content.text:
On CoSy as one file, browser upload and storage, by measurement:

**Sizes** (from `ba-cosy-zip-fork/reva-fork-subset/build`, the package that runs on reva-fork):

| What | Size |
|---|---|
| CoSy's Forth code (CoSy.f, Furniture.f, util.f, Tui.f and others) | 161 KB |
| CoSy.csy, the state CoSy loads at start | 67 KB |
| Optional `.csy` data: WorkLog, Presentations, ForthDay15, MinJob | 586 + 202 + 139 + 22 KB |
| help.txt, cosy.png | 116 KB, 147 KB |
| The whole package directory | 1.5 MB |
| The turtle fractals example (cosy-fractals.f) | 4 KB |

So CoSy itself, code plus its starting state, is about 230 KB.

**Browser storage:** `localStorage` holds about 5 MB per origin. The catch is the origin: it's `softwarewrighter.github.io`, shared by every project demo there, and the page stores files as text, one character per byte. CoSy's 230 KB fits easily, and even the whole package would. For real use I'd move the page's file storage to IndexedDB or the Origin Private File System, which allow hundreds of MB or more per origin and store bytes directly.

**One file for CLI and desktop:** two ways.
- **Bundle the source:** inline CoSy.f's `include`s into one `cosy.f` of about 230 KB, with the starting state embedded or loaded beside it. Then `include cosy.f` or `reva cosy.f`.
- **A saved image:** load CoSy once, then `save cosy.img`. reva-fork already starts from images: `reva --image cosy.img`, and the browser's `?image=`. That's one file with the fastest start; I haven't measured its size yet.

Either is the CoSy lane's work, since the local lane doesn't edit ba-cosy-zip-fork. reva-fork's part is making images and uploads work well everywhere.

**Upload in the browser:** yes, in your two steps:
1. An Upload button on the page puts the chosen files into the page's file system, where they're saved in storage.
2. Then `include CoSy.f` at the prompt, as on the CLI. Later uploads, such as more `.csy` files or examples, work the same way.

Because users upload their own copy, our published site doesn't redistribute CoSy, which fits your earlier rule.

**Proposed new saga steps** (I'll add them if you agree, after step 32):
- `local-web-upload`: an Upload button and IndexedDB storage for the page's files, with a size readout.
- `local-image-everywhere`: check saving and starting from images on all three hosts, and measure a CoSy image, as input for the CoSy lane.

Step 30 (`local-help`): the gate is running, and I'll commit and open the PR when it passes. Help now shows real documentation in all three hosts, including the browser. The golden `help-content` covers real descriptions and finds all 1,377 documented words.

content.text:
Yes. GitHub Pages supports exactly that:
1. **A public repo** (e.g. the CoSy fork, or a small `cosy-web` repo) publishes a static site on its `gh-pages` branch. ba-cosy-zip-fork already has the pieces: `make-cosy-zip.sh` builds reva-fork's web page with the CoSy package preloaded, and the page starts it. Starting from a saved image instead (the page's `?image=`) would skip loading CoSy's sources and make startup almost instant.
2. **DNS:** a CNAME record `cosy.softwarewrighter.com → softwarewrighter.github.io`, which you'd add at your DNS provider.
3. **Pages settings:** set the custom domain (it writes a `CNAME` file into the site) and tick "Enforce HTTPS". GitHub issues the certificate.

**A real bonus:** its own origin. Today every demo under `softwarewrighter.github.io` shares one browser storage quota, and those pages could read each other's saved files. `cosy.softwarewrighter.com` gets its own storage, so CoSy's saved `.csy` files and history stay private to it, with the full ~5 MB of `localStorage`, or far more once the page uses IndexedDB.

**Two things to decide first:**
- **Redistribution.** Publishing CoSy's sources or an image on a public site distributes Bob Armstrong's code. You've said you generally don't want to redistribute code, so that needs his terms or permission, or the upload approach instead: the site ships reva-fork plus a "load CoSy" step that takes the user's own copy.
- **Who does it.** The CoSy site belongs to the CoSy lane, since this lane doesn't edit ba-cosy-zip-fork. reva-fork's part would be small: let `scripts/publish-pages.sh` (or `make-web-zip.sh`) take a package or image and a custom domain (writing the `CNAME` file), so any package can be published this way.

# The browser REPL as a static site

Reva runs in the browser as a WebAssembly VM in a Web Worker
(`components/web/crates/reva-web/www`). This page covers what a page can be told through its
URL, the split view, loading a package from a static directory, and
building the zip you upload to a web host.

```text
just web-zip                      # or: scripts/make-web-zip.sh
#   → target/web/reva-web-VERSION.zip   (and the same tree, unzipped, beside it)
# upload, unzip anywhere on the host, open https://your.host/any/path/reva-web-VERSION/
```

## URL options

| Option | Effect |
|---|---|
| `?canvas=split` | REPL on the left, turtle graphics on the right (below) |
| `?canvas=pane` | graphics in a pane below the REPL |
| `?canvas=window` | graphics in a popup window (the default; a pane where popups are blocked) |
| `?package=DIR/` | load the package in `DIR` (relative to the page) |
| `?include=FILE` | include FILE after start and after each `restart` (repeatable) |
| `?eval=TEXT` | feed TEXT once after start (repeatable) |
| `?image=FILE` | start from a saved image instead of booting `reva.f` |

When the URL does not say, the page falls back to the package's `canvas`,
then to its own default: the `reva-canvas` meta tag in `index.html`, which
the web zip sets to `split`. Likewise the `reva-package` meta tag names the
package to open when there is no `?package=`.

## The split view

`?canvas=split` (or `"canvas": "split"` in a package manifest) shows the
REPL and the graphics pane side by side, both full height, 50/50 to start.

- **Drag the divider** to resize; the REPL's share stays within 20–80%.
- **Keyboard:** Tab to the divider, then ←/→ move it 2% (Shift: 10%),
  Home/End go to the limits, Enter collapses or restores the pane.
- **Double-click** the divider to go back to 50/50.
- **Collapse:** the ⟩ button folds the graphics pane to a strip at the right
  edge; the strip's button brings it back.
- **Remembered:** position and collapsed state are kept in localStorage
  (`reva:ui:split`) for the site's origin.
- **Redraws on resize:** the drawing is redrawn at the pane's new
  resolution once a resize settles (120 ms).
- Under 640 px wide the panes stack, REPL above graphics.

The desktop app shows the same split with `--canvas split` or a package's
`"canvas": "split"` (see [desktop.md](desktop.md)).

## The About dialog

The **About** button in the header opens a dialog with:

- the package's entry, when a package is open (from its manifest's
  `about`, below);
- then reva-fork's: version, credits, links to the source and docs, and
  the licenses (`LICENSE`, `LICENSE-MIT`, `docs/licenses.md` on GitHub);
- the build: `VERSION COMMIT DATE` from the page's `reva-build` meta tag,
  which `make-web-zip.sh` and `components/desktop/build.sh` stamp
  (`scripts/build-stamp.sh`; `-dirty` marks uncommitted changes). From
  the source tree it says "development build".

Esc, the Close button or a click outside closes it. It is the same in the
zips, in reva-serve binaries and in the desktop app, where links open in the
system browser.

## SQLite in the browser

`needs db/sqlite` works on the page: the VM's worker loads SQLite's
official WebAssembly build from jsDelivr the first time a program uses
SQLite (`sqlite.js`; pinned, about 1.5 MB, cached by the browser after the
first time, and not part of this site) and keeps databases in the
browser's private file system. See [sqlite.md](sqlite.md). The About
dialog credits it. Offline (the downloaded zip, `reva-serve` without a
network) SQLite stops with a note; the desktop app has its own SQLite.

## The footer

A line under the REPL shows the copyright, the license, a link to the
source, and which build of the VM is running: version, commit, build host
and build time (hover for the license in full and the exact time). These
come from the WebAssembly module (`reva_build_info_ptr`/`_len`, from
`reva_vm::version`), so they are what `reva -V` and `version` print for
the same build. `components/web/crates/reva-web/index.html` and `favicon.ico` are symlinks
into `www/` for sw-checklist, which looks for them in the crate folder.

## Packages from a static directory: `?package=DIR/`

`DIR/reva-package.json` is the manifest the [desktop app](desktop.md) reads
with `--package DIR`, plus a `files` list, since a static server cannot list
a folder:

```json
{
  "name": "CoSy",
  "title": "CoSy",
  "icon": "cosy.png",
  "id": "cosy",
  "canvas": "split",
  "start": ["start-cosy.f"],
  "files": ["CoSy.f", "util.f", "start-cosy.f"]
}
```

| Key | In the browser |
|---|---|
| `files` | fetched (six at a time) into the VM at `/<file>`, as the desktop app maps the package folder to `/`; a file that fails is a note, not a stop |
| `start` | fetched too, and included after start and after each `restart` |
| `title` | page title and header (default `<name> on Reva`) |
| `icon` | the page's icon (favicon) |
| `id` | names the localStorage prefix, `reva:<id>:fs:` (default from `name`), so two packages on one site keep their files apart |
| `canvas` | where graphics go, unless the URL says |
| `about` | the package's entry in the About dialog: `{ "name", "version", "description", "build", "credits": [text], "links": [{ "label", "url" }] }`, all optional (`name` defaults to `title`; `build` is the package's own commit and date, so a bug report names both layers); only http(s) links become links |
| `hint` | replaces Reva's hint in the page header; `` `code` `` in backticks |

Paths must be plain relative paths (no `..`, no leading `/`); others are
skipped with a note. Files the VM writes are stored in localStorage and win
over the package's copy on the next load, so edits survive a reload. The
desktop app ignores `files` (it reads the folder itself).

## The uploadable zip: `just web-zip`

`scripts/make-web-zip.sh` (POSIX sh; `just web-zip` runs it) builds
`reva.wasm` and writes `target/web/NAME-web-VERSION.zip`, holding one
folder `NAME-web-VERSION/`:

```text
index.html  reva.js  reva-worker.js  reva.wasm  host.js  ui.js  canvas.html
split.js  package.js  README.txt  LICENSE.txt  LICENSE-MIT.txt  [pkg/ ...]
```

| Option | Effect |
|---|---|
| `--package DIR` | copy DIR into `pkg/` and open it by default; NAME defaults to its `id` |
| `--canvas MODE` | the default graphics placement (default `split`) |
| `--name NAME`, `--version V` | the zip's name (default `reva`, the workspace version) |
| `--out DIR` | where the zip goes (default `target/web`) |
| `--no-build` | use the `reva.wasm` already built |

With `just`: `just web-zip --package path/to/pkg`. CoSy's zip is built in
its own repository (`just cosy-zip` in ba-cosy-zip-fork), which calls this
script.

To check a zip the way a web host serves it, unzip it into a subdirectory
of any static server:

```text
mkdir -p /tmp/site/a/b && cd /tmp/site/a/b && unzip ~/reva-web-VERSION.zip
python3 -m http.server -d /tmp/site 8000
#   open http://localhost:8000/a/b/reva-web-VERSION/
```

`file://` does not work: browsers do not start module workers or fetch
files from `file://` pages. To run the same tree with no server at all,
use [reva-serve](serve.md), which embeds it in one binary.

## The live demo: `just publish`

The plain reva-fork REPL (no package) is published at
<https://softwarewrighter.github.io/reva-fork/> by `just publish`
(`scripts/publish-pages.sh`): it builds the static site with
`make-web-zip.sh` (split view by default), adds `.nojekyll`, and
force-pushes it as one orphan commit to the `gh-pages` branch, which GitHub
Pages serves. Only `main` is published: the tree must be clean and HEAD on
`origin/main`, so the footer's build commit is a released one.
`just publish --dry-run` builds the commit from any HEAD and pushes nothing.

Every `softwarewrighter.github.io` project page shares one origin, so the
demo's saved files and history (`reva:` keys in `localStorage`) share the
storage quota with the other projects' demos there, and those pages could
read them.

## Design notes

* **Static and relative, on purpose.** Every URL the page uses is relative to
  `index.html` (`reva.wasm`, `pkg/...`), there is no server logic, and no
  special headers: no SharedArrayBuffer, so no COOP/COEP, which ISP hosts
  rarely let you set. So the same tree works from an ISP's shared hosting,
  GitHub Pages, `python3 -m http.server`, or embedded in `reva-serve`.
* **The manifest is the one contract.** The desktop app, the browser and
  the zip read the same `reva-package.json`; `files` is the only key the
  browser needs that the desktop does not.
* **Defaults in meta tags, not code.** The zip is `www/` plus a package,
  with two `<meta>` values set (`reva-package`, `reva-canvas`). No build
  step rewrites JavaScript, and a URL option still overrides either.
* **Files are per origin.** localStorage belongs to scheme + host + port. A
  site moved to another host starts with no saved files, and the split
  position is remembered per origin too. Storage is optional: where a
  browser blocks it the page says so and works without it.
* **Reproducible zip.** Names are sorted and every entry carries the last
  commit's time, so one commit gives one zip (same SHA-256), which makes a
  zip on a web host easy to match with its source.
* **Resize redraw without a copy.** The graphics page keeps no copy of the
  drawing: on resize it sizes its backing store to the pane and asks the
  VM to send the drawing again (the same `resend` used when a window
  opens), so memory stays bounded and the lines stay sharp at any size.
* **About text is data, not markup.** The manifest's `about` goes into the
  page with `textContent` only, and a link is made only from an http(s)
  URL, so a package cannot inject HTML or a `javascript:` link. The
  desktop's `open_url` command refuses other schemes too.
* **Typing before boot.** Lines entered while a package is still loading
  are queued and fed after its start files.

The original Reva drew inside the dialog, in an IUP **canvas element**. There was no separate pane:
- A program put `canvas[ ... ]w` into its dialog's boxes like any other control, alongside labels and buttons, and the dialog was a native window. `binary-clock.f`, for example, has three canvases in a row, one each for hours, minutes and seconds.
- It drew with Tecgraf's **CD** library (`lib/ui/cd`: lines, boxes, arcs, text, colours) from the canvas's redraw callback. IUP called the callback whenever the canvas needed painting, so the program redrew from its own state; nothing kept a drawing.
- OpenGL worked the same way through `IupGLCanvas` (`gl-test.f`).
- **CoSy's Tui.f has no graphics at all:** its notebook is text panes, labels and buttons only.
- **Turtle graphics in a separate pane or window is reva-fork's own addition** (2026-10-25). It isn't original Reva; the original had no turtle library.

So the faithful route for drawing in a dialog is step 37 (`local-ui-canvas`), formerly 33: canvas elements drawn in place by a virtual CD library, giving binary-clock, brownian and cd-test. A notebook could then also have a drawing pane of its own. Today's split view (notebook beside the turtle pane) is a reva-fork convenience on top.

Step 31 (`local-notebook-web`) is done apart from its gate, which is running. All three requirements work in the browser build, checked in Chrome:
- `needs ui/notebook notebook` loads.
- The text persists in local storage across a reload, now covered by a smoke-test check.
- The notebook sits in the REPL column, with turtle drawings appearing in the graphics pane beside it.

The live demo gets this with the next release.

# Reva Forth — portable core

A Rust port of the Reva Forth core that runs on any 64-bit host and in the
browser (WebAssembly), while running Reva's own Forth source — including the
words written as x86 machine code — unchanged.

It does this by executing the small subset of 32-bit x86 that Reva's compiler
and primitives use (a "vx86" VM), with the assembly core's routines
re-implemented in Rust. See [design.md](../docs/design.md) for the rationale.

## Status

- All of `src/reva.f` boots verbatim (assembler, contexts, `needs`, the
  FFI layer, the Linux personality) and restarts as its saved executable
  did: banner, `ok>` prompt, `reva.f`'s error handling. See design.md §3.6.
- `needs` loads libraries from `lib/` (via the virtual prefix `/reva/lib/`;
  set `$REVA_HOME` to use another tree).
- A virtual libc (`getenv`, `putenv`, `localtime`, `opendir`/`readdir`)
  and a portable `syscall` subset; `time&date`, `ms@`, `getenv` work.
- File words (`open/r`, `read`, `seek`, `stat`, `rename`, …) through
  `Host::fs`: real files on the CLI, an in-memory file system in the
  browser (kept in `localStorage`); `lib/` is built in. See design.md §3.7.
- Hosts: `reva` CLI (Linux/macOS/Windows, any CPU) and a WebAssembly module
  with a minimal web console; the VM runs in a Web Worker with time slices
  and a Stop button (design.md §3.8).
- Saved images: `save NAME` from Forth or `reva --save-image`; start one
  with `reva --image` or in the browser (`start(..., { image })`).
  `restart` makes the VM again the same way (design.md §3.9).
- x87 floating point with `f64` registers and 80-bit memory operands;
  `lib/math/floats` passes its own tests (design.md §3.10).
- Not yet: native libraries, native translation. See the roadmap in design.md.

## Layout

One Cargo workspace per component (the rules: [code-metrics.md](../docs/code-metrics.md)),
each `components/<name>/` with its `Cargo.toml`, `Cargo.lock` and
`crates/<crate>/`. All of them build into the repository's `target/`.

```
components/
  macros/   reva-macros  machine_trait!, words!, ext_trait!
  x86-types/  reva-x86-base, -mem, -fpustate, -types   faults, layout, memory, x87 registers, Op/Insn/Cpu
  x86-decode/ reva-x86-cursor, -opcodes, -fpudec, -decode   the decoder (an opcode table)
  x86-alu/    reva-x86-ops, -shift, -float              operands, ALU, shifts, strings, x87 math
  x86-exec/   reva-x86-fpuexec, -exec                   executing instructions
  x86/      reva-x86     facade: the x86 components under their old paths
  host-base/ reva-version, -embedded, -hostcall, -charset   build stamp, reva.f and lib/, host calls, encodings
  vfs/      reva-vfs, reva-memtree, reva-memfs         file-system traits, the in-memory file system
  host/     reva-host-traits, -buffer, reva-host       the Host traits, BufferHost, a facade at the old paths
  core-parts/ reva-gate, reva-heap, reva-translate   gates, the heap allocator, translator hooks
  canvas/   reva-canvas, reva-canvas-out           the turtle's display list; ops for windows, SVG
  ui/       reva-ui-base, -text, -tree, reva-ui   the model of IUP programs' UIs (../docs/ui-model.md)
  ui-layout/ reva-ui-layout   IUP's layout of the model, in character cells
  ui-grid/  reva-ui-mirror, -grid, -paint   the TUI: the model painted into character cells
  ui-web/   reva-ui-web     the TUI in the page (Yew; scripts/build-web.sh)
  iup/      reva-vlib-iup, reva-ui-script   the virtual library iup; a scripted headless UI host
  core/     reva-core, -ffi, -inspect              the Machine and its helpers; (call) args; dictionary, state
  core-run/ reva-core-run, reva-core-boot          the run loop; new machines and images
  vlib/     reva-vlib-turtle, -highlight, -iconv, reva-vlib   virtual libraries (reva-vlib: the old paths)
  words-base/   reva-words-code, -text, -calls, -scan   the words' helpers
  words-interp/ reva-words-classes, -interp, -eval      classes, interpreter, eval, catch, defining
  words-dict/   reva-words-compile, -memory, -system    compiling, numbers, memory, bye/version
  words-os/     reva-words-sys, -files, -libc, -ffi     system calls, file words, libc, (call)
  words/    reva-words   the dispatch table: every gate to its handler
  vm/       reva-vm      the facade the front ends use (re-exports, Machine with
                         dispatch installed; ../docs/design.md 3.12)
  sqlite/   reva-sqlite, reva-vlib-sqlite   SQLite (rusqlite, safe API); the virtual library
  cli-edit/ reva-keys, -history, -lineedit, -rawterm   the terminal line editor
  cli-host/ reva-hostpath, -stdfs, -term, -stdhost     the command-line host
  cli/      reva-cli     the `reva` command: options, run, session
  web/      reva-web-state, -run, -io, reva-web   wasm32 module + www/ (reva.js,
                         index.html) + test/*.mjs
  serve/    reva-serve-http, reva-serve   one-binary local web app: embeds a site,
                         serves 127.0.0.1 (std only; ../docs/serve.md)
  desktop/  reva-desktop-pkg, -state, reva-desktop   the Tauri app, with build.sh,
                         smoke.sh, host.js
scripts/      build-web.sh, regress.sh, add-regress.sh, check.sh, bench-guard.sh,
              doc-check.sh (run docs/ samples), parity-examples.sh, ...
tests/forth/  Forth scripts used by the regression suite
work/reg-rs/  reg-rs regression tests (.rgt specs + golden .out/.err)
```

## Build and run

From the repository root:

```bash
just cli                                  # or: cargo build --release --manifest-path components/cli/Cargo.toml
target/release/reva                       # REPL (ok> prompt)
target/release/reva file.f -e '...'       # include files, evaluate text
echo ': sq dup * ; 7 sq .' | target/release/reva
target/release/reva --help
```

WebAssembly:

```bash
scripts/build-web.sh                      # → components/web/crates/reva-web/www/reva.wasm
python3 -m http.server -d components/web/crates/reva-web/www    # open http://localhost:8000
node components/web/crates/reva-web/test/smoke.mjs              # headless check
scripts/make-web-zip.sh                   # → target/web/reva-web-VERSION.zip (../docs/web.md)
scripts/build-serve.sh                    # → target/serve/reva-serve-VERSION-TARGET (../docs/serve.md)
```

## Tests

The gate before every commit, from the repository root:

```bash
just check            # fmt, clippy, tests, wasm + node tests, desktop, goldens, licenses, sw-checklist
just check --fast     # the same without the desktop component
```

`scripts/check.sh` lists the goldens known to fail on each OS (the list
may only shrink) and requires sw-checklist to report no FAILs.

Refactors of hot code (gate dispatch, decode, exec) also run the timing
guard before and after:

```bash
just bench-guard            # boot, fib, a loop, dragons: medians vs this host's baseline
just bench-guard --record   # (re)record this host's baseline in work/bench-guard.txt
```

It fails when a median is more than 15% (`TOLERANCE`) slower than the
host's recorded baseline; timings only compare on the same machine, so
each host has its own lines. It is not part of `just check` (it takes
about 17 s and timing is noisy on a busy machine). The pieces of the
gate:

```bash
just test                                 # unit + API tests, every component
scripts/regress.sh                        # reg-rs golden-output suite
scripts/regress.sh -vv -p core-catch      # one test, full diff on failure
REVA=target/release/reva scripts/regress.sh
```

The regression suite uses [reg-rs](https://github.com/sw-cli-tools/reg-rs)
(`reg-rs` on PATH, or `REG_RS=/path/to/reg-rs`). Add a test with

```bash
scripts/add-regress.sh NAME '${REVA:-target/debug/reva} < tests/forth/NAME.f' 'what it covers'
```

and review the captured `work/reg-rs/NAME.out` before committing: a baseline
asserts the output is *correct*. Accept an intended change with
`REG_RS_DATA_DIR=work/reg-rs reg-rs rebase -p NAME`.

Source as color-highlighted HTML or PNG, for slides, docs and blog figures
(Python 3 standard library; `--png` uses headless Chrome or Chromium):

```bash
scripts/forth-highlight.py lib/turtle/fractals --lines 22-30 --title 'Koch' --png koch.png
```

Documentation lives in [`../docs/`](../docs/README.md); its Forth samples are
checked by `scripts/doc-check.sh docs/*.md`, and
`scripts/parity-examples.sh` reports how far every program in `examples/`
gets (both are part of the regression suite).

The scripts filter text with [sed-rs](https://github.com/sw-cli-tools/sed-rs)
(`cargo install --path .` in its checkout, or set `$SED_RS`), never the
system sed, so they behave the same on every platform. Patterns use
sed-rs syntax: Rust regex, where `( ) | + ?` are operators; write a
literal one as a bracket (`[(]`, `[?]`).

## Debugging

- Faults name the Forth word: `*** bad memory access ... (in bad+0xc, ...)`.
- `reva --trace` logs every step to stderr.
- Code the core cannot run (native libraries, `shell`, MMX/SSE and
  privileged instructions) stops with a message pointing to
  [docs/portability.md](../docs/portability.md); `reva --allow-shell` lets
  `shell` run OS commands.
- `cargo run -p reva-vm --example probe -- ': f 1 2 + ;' 'see f'` runs
  lines and disassembles words.

## License

MIT, Copyright (c) 2026 Michael A. Wright, for the code in this
directory (see [LICENSE](LICENSE)). The Reva
Forth sources it embeds and runs (`src/reva.f`) remain in the public domain
under the original terms; see [../LICENSING.md](../LICENSING.md).

# Plan: IUP programs (and CoSy's TUI) on reva-fork

High-level plan for running Reva's IUP GUI programs on the portable core,
CoSy's "Textual User Interface" (`Tui.f`) first among them. What needs to
be done, in what order, and how we will know it works. The low-level
design (components, crates, modules, files) comes later, after the
sw-checklist work, within the rules in CLAUDE.md. Saga steps:
`local-ui-model`, `local-iup`, `local-ui-grid`, `local-ui-terminal`,
`local-tui-cosy`, `local-ui-canvas` (stage 1; the terminal backend before
`Tui.f`, so the first TUI demo runs in all three hosts); `local-ui-panes`
(stage 2).

## Goal

Existing Reva GUI programs run **unchanged** on reva-fork: in the browser,
in the desktop app and on the live demo, and the Notebook (below) in the
CLI's terminal too. The Forth side (`lib/ui/iup`, `lib/ui/gui`, the
programs) is not edited.

## Two stages (the user, 2026-10-30)

1. **The Notebook: parity first.** What Reva and CoSy did with IUP.
   CoSy's `Tui.f` is a notebook: one dialog with three edit panes (the
   text you type, the result of evaluating it, a state pane), a stack
   status line, a row of buttons, and F-keys (F6 evaluates the current
   line, shift-F6 the selection, F8/F9 send a line elsewhere, others
   insert dates or save the text into CoSy's dictionary). Reva's own
   `examples/iup` are single dialogs of widgets. Stage 1 runs both in the
   browser, the desktop app, and (without graphics) the CLI's terminal.
2. **Panes: a longer-term goal** that builds on stage 1, not the other
   way round. A tmux/Emacs-inspired layout: split horizontally and
   vertically, zoom one pane to the full window and back; an editor pane
   (load, save, evaluate a line into a REPL), a tail pane (follow a file
   or another pane's output), several REPLs, IUP dialogs in panes; the
   same layout in the browser, the desktop app and the terminal.

## Decisions (with the user, 2026-10-28)

- **Reimplement, do not wrap or redistribute.** IUP (Tecgraf/PUC-Rio) is
  a C toolkit; the core cannot call native code, and we do not ship it.
  We implement, in Rust, the part of IUP's C API that Reva's libraries
  call, as a *virtual library* (the pattern of iconv and SQLite).
- **Rendered with Rust/Yew**, in the web page and the desktop app (which
  shows the same page).
- **In reva-fork.** `lib/ui/gui` is a Reva library; every IUP program
  benefits, CoSy is one user. ba-cosy-zip-fork then only drops its "no
  GUI" patches.
- **After the component restructuring** (saga steps `local-components`
  to `local-comp-front-ends`), so the new code starts in the new shape.

## What Reva programs use (the scope)

| Layer | What | Size |
|---|---|---|
| `lib/ui/iup` | binds the IUP C libraries (`libiup`, `libiupcd`, `libiupcontrols`, `libiupgl`) through `lib`/`func:` | ~75 C functions |
| `lib/ui/gui` | the Forth vocabulary (Danny Reinhold): `dialog[ … ]d`, `vbox[`/`hbox[`, `button[`, `label[`, `editbox[`, `attr:`, `action:`, `gui-main-loop` … | 136 words |
| programs | 20 in `examples/iup/`, and CoSy's `Tui.f` | 21 programs |

The 21 programs use **70 of the 136 words**. Every one builds a dialog
and runs `gui-main-loop`; most use buttons, labels, boxes and actions:

- **Core** (most programs): `dialog[ ]d`, `button[`, `label[`, `hbox[`
  `hboxs[` `vbox[` `vboxs[`, `spacer`, `frame[`, `title`, `size`,
  `expand`, `tip`, `attr:`, `action:`, `action[`, `show`, `popup`,
  `gui-main-loop`, `getval`/`setval`.
- **Text editing** (Tui.f and 2 examples): `editbox[`, `text[`, `caret?`,
  `caret-y?`, `selection?`, `selected-text?`, `line-text?`, key callbacks
  (`K_F1`…`K_F12`, `K_cS`, `key-any-cb:`).
- **Dialogs**: `file-open-dialog[`, `file-save-dialog[`, message boxes.
- **Menus and bars**: `menu[`, `menu-item[`, `menu-separator`,
  `]submenu`, `toolbar[`.
- **Other controls**: `toggle[`, `radio[`, lists, tabs, `matrix[`
  (IupControls), timers (`timer`, `set-time`, `start-timer`).
- **Drawing**: `canvas[` with the CD drawing library (4 programs), images
  (`ui/gui-iup-img`, 3), OpenGL (1).

CoSy's `Tui.f` needs 33 words: the core set, text editing with F-keys,
`file-open-dialog[`, `popup`/`show-xy`/`hide`/`destroy`, `topmost`, and
one direct `IupStoreAttribute`.

## Work, in order

1. **UI model** (`local-ui-model`). A Rust model of IUP's world, with no
   VM and no rendering: the element tree (dialogs, boxes, controls),
   attributes by IUP's names and its inheritance rules, callbacks by
   name, the layout IUP computes (natural size, `EXPAND`, `SIZE`,
   margins and gaps), and a stream of changes a renderer applies.
   Tested on its own. Done: components `ui` and `ui-layout`; scope and
   rules in [ui-model.md](ui-model.md).
2. **The `iup` virtual library** (`local-iup`). The C functions above,
   answered in the VM over that model; handles are integers, strings
   copied, so no pointer crosses. Events: `IupMainLoop` and `IupPopup`
   wait for the user, as a host call that pauses the VM (the way SQLite
   calls pause in the desktop app); when an event arrives, the Forth
   callback runs, and its result (`IUP_DEFAULT`, `IUP_CLOSE`, ...)
   decides what happens next. A headless host drives events in tests.
   Done: component `iup`; see [ui-model.md](ui-model.md#the-virtual-library-iup).
3. **The renderer: one TUI everywhere** (`local-ui-grid`; decided with
   the user 2026-10-31). The model lays out into a grid of character
   cells (text, colour, cursor), pure Rust with goldens on the grid. Thin
   backends draw it: a monospace grid element in the web page (the
   desktop app shows the same page), and crossterm in the CLI's terminal
   (step 5). Keys (function keys included), mouse and resize go back as
   events. crossterm alone cannot do it: it needs a real terminal and does
   not build for wasm; the grid makes the look the same in all three.
   Done: components `ui-grid` and `ui-web`; see
   [ui-model.md](ui-model.md#the-tui).
4. **CoSy's TUI end to end** (`local-tui-cosy`). `Tui.f` running
   unchanged in the desktop app and the browser; whatever it still needs
   fixed here; the CoSy lane told what to drop.
5. **The terminal backend** (`local-ui-terminal`): the grid in the CLI
   through crossterm (raw mode, keys, mouse, resize, redrawing changed
   cells): `Tui.f` and the simple examples in a terminal.
6. **Graphics** (`local-ui-canvas`; browser and desktop only). Reva drew
   through IUP's `canvas[` and Tecgraf's CD library (`lib/ui/cd`: lines,
   boxes, arcs, polygons, text, colours, clipping, images), repainting
   from the canvas's redraw callback. CD becomes a virtual library that
   draws into the turtle's display list (components/canvas), shown by a
   canvas pane; parity: `binary-clock`, `brownian`, `cd-test`. Not CD's
   PDF/printer contexts, and not OpenGL.
7. **The rest of the examples**, in order of how many programs a feature
   unblocks: menus and toolbars, toggles, radios, lists and tabs, timers,
   file and message dialogs, the matrix; then drawing (the CD library on
   the turtle canvas's drawing surface), images; OpenGL last, if at all.

## How we will know it works

- Goldens (CLI, headless host): building and querying dialogs, attribute
  values, callbacks fired by scripted events, for `examples/iup/`'s
  simple programs and a scripted Tui-like session.
- The web smoke test: the renderer's DOM for a known model; events back.
- Manual checks in Chrome and the desktop app on the Mac, with
  screenshots, for each phase.
- The parity report: the 20 IUP examples move from "could not load
  IupOpen" to running, phase by phase.

## Open questions

- **The CLI.** Decided: the same cell grid through crossterm (step 5),
  without graphics.
- **Look.** Decided: a text-mode TUI, the same in every host, coloured
  with the REPL page's themes (light and dark). HTML widgets maybe later.
- **Windows.** One dialog at a time inside the page, several as in-page
  windows, or separate native windows in the desktop app (as the turtle
  graphics window)?
- **Drawing (CD) and images.** Decided: the turtle's display list, in a
  canvas pane (step 6).
- **Licensing of names.** IUP's API names and behaviour are reimplemented
  from its documentation (MIT); nothing of its code. To record in
  docs/licenses.md when the work starts.

## Risks

- IUP's layout rules are detailed; programs that depend on exact pixel
  sizes may look different. Mitigation: implement IUP's documented
  algorithm, compare with screenshots of the original where we have
  them.
- Callback-heavy programs (timers, key-any) stress the pause/resume
  path; the bench guard and the smoke test watch it.
- Scope creep across 136 words and IUP's controls library: phase 5 is
  ordered by programs unblocked, and stops where the examples stop.

through IUP's `canvas[` and Tecgraf's CD library (`lib/ui/cd`: lines,

content.content:
## Turtle fractals, the CoSy way

`cosy-fractals.f` draws fractals in reva-fork's graphics window (needs
reva-fork with turtle graphics, PR #20; see its `docs/turtle.md`):

```sh
./cosy-desktop -e 'include cosy-fractals.f' -e '12 cdragon'
```

then `5 ckoch`, `6 chilbert`, `7 csierpinski`, `12 cdragon` at `ok>`. Each
prints its segment count, then draws. On the CLI (`build/run-cosy`) there
is no window: `" dragon.svg" svg-save .` writes the drawing as SVG.

reva-fork's Forth versions (`needs turtle/fractals`) draw *while they
recurse*: one turtle call per segment. Here the curve is **data first**, built
## The web demo zip

A zip you upload to any web host, unzip (a subfolder is fine), and open in a
browser: CoSy on reva-fork's WebAssembly VM, with the REPL on the left and
the turtle graphics on the right.

```sh
just cosy-zip                        # or: reva-fork-subset/make-cosy-zip.sh
#   → ../reva-fork/rust/target/web/cosy-web-VERSION.zip
```

It needs a reva-fork checkout beside this one (`../reva-fork`, on `dev`;
or set `REVA_FORK`) with Rust and rustup, plus `perl` and `zip`. The script
builds `build/` (make-subset.sh), then runs reva-fork's
`rust/scripts/make-web-zip.sh --package build --name cosy`, which builds
`reva.wasm` and writes the zip. Options pass through, e.g. `just cosy-zip
--version 2026.1028.0` or `--out ~/Desktop`.

Upload and try it:

```text
### cosy-serve: the same, as one binary

`cosy-serve` holds the web demo and a tiny web server in one file. Run it
and CoSy opens in your browser from http://127.0.0.1:8481/, with the REPL on
the left and the turtle graphics on the right. Ctrl-C stops it. Files you
write are kept by the browser for that address, so they are there on the
next run. A second launch just opens the browser on the running one.

```sh
just cosy-serve              # or: reva-fork-subset/make-cosy-serve.sh
#   macOS: universal binary (arm64 + x86_64); Linux: static musl binary
just cosy-serve linux windows   # on Linux: also a Windows .exe (needs mingw-w64)
#   → ../reva-fork/rust/target/serve/cosy-serve-VERSION-TARGET[.exe] (+ .sha256)
../reva-fork/rust/target/serve/cosy-serve-*-macos-universal     # run it
```

## What CoSy still needs from reva-fork

The CLI, the desktop app, the web zip and cosy-serve all run this subset.
What is missing (the IUP windows of Tui.f and Job.f, `help`, `shell>`,
opening a URL) needs work in reva-fork; see
[../docs/reva-fork-asks.md](../docs/reva-fork-asks.md) for symptoms,
repros and suggested fixes.

cd "$(dirname "$0")" || exit 1
REVA=${REVA:-reva}
REVA_HISTORY=${REVA_HISTORY-$HOME/.cosy_history}
export REVA_HISTORY
while :; do
  "$REVA" start-cosy.f "$@"
  status=$?
  [ $status -eq 3 ] || exit $status
  echo "--- restarting CoSy ---"
done
---
set -e
HERE=$(cd "$(dirname "$0")" && pwd)
APP=${REVA_DESKTOP:-reva-desktop}
command -v "$APP" >/dev/null 2>&1 || {
  echo "cosy-desktop: $APP not found; install reva-fork's desktop app or set REVA_DESKTOP" >&2
  exit 127
}
[ -f "$HERE/build/reva-package.json" ] || "$HERE/make-subset.sh" >&2
newer=$(find "$HERE" "$HERE/../sample/CoSy" "$HERE/../VERSION" -maxdepth 1 -type f \
  -newer "$HERE/build/reva-package.json" 2>/dev/null | head -n 1)
[ -z "$newer" ] || echo "cosy-desktop: build/ is older than ${newer#$HERE/}; to update it, run $HERE/make-subset.sh (it replaces build/, saved .csy files included)" >&2
exec "$APP" --package "$HERE/build" "$@"

content.text: so Ctrl-Enter and Cmd-Enter do not work at the CLI.  Fn-F6 works.
they are used by Mac

That's how terminals work: they send the same byte for Enter and Ctrl-Enter, and Cmd-Enter belongs to the terminal app. For the CLI I want a key that a terminal can tell apart and that sits near the home row. Ctrl-J sends a different byte from Enter in raw mode (linefeed rather than carriage return), but it depends on how crossterm decodes it. Checking crossterm's input parser:

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Run a command in a fresh temporary directory, then remove it, so a test
# that writes files (the notebook's notebook.txt, ...) never touches the
# checkout.  REVA (default target/debug/reva) and ROOT (the checkout) are
# exported as absolute paths; the command's exit status is the script's.
#
#   scripts/in-tempdir.sh sh -c '"$REVA" --ui-script "$ROOT/tests/ui/x.ui" < /dev/null'
set -u
ROOT=$(cd "$(dirname "$0")/.." && pwd)
REVA=${REVA:-target/debug/reva}
case "$REVA" in /*) ;; *) REVA="$ROOT/$REVA" ;; esac
export ROOT REVA
dir=$(mktemp -d) || exit 1
(cd "$dir" && "$@")
status=$?
rm -rf "$dir"
exit $status

# Personal instructions

## Python
- Never use the system `python3` (Xcode/Homebrew/user-site) for anything: not for running
  project code, scratch experiments, or one-off text edits.
- Always create the environment with `uv venv` and install packages with `uv pip install ...`.
- Run Python via `.venv/bin/python` (or `uv run`). If `.venv` is missing, create it first.

# reva-fork -- Claude Instructions

## Baseline expectations for agentrail-driven sessions

You are working with the agentrail saga/steps process. The saga record (the
`.agentrail/` directory) is the durable handoff between sessions — if your
work is not reflected there, the next session cannot see it.

Before reporting work as complete:

- Confirm the active step is reflected in `.agentrail/` and committed.
- Run the project's pre-commit gate (tests, lint, format) before
  `agentrail complete`, not after.
- If you discover unplanned work, prefer `agentrail insert` / `agentrail add`
  over silently doing it inside another step.

## CRITICAL: Agentrail session protocol (follow exactly)

Every session follows this sequence. Do not skip steps, do not reorder.

### 1. START — `agentrail next`
First thing in the session. Read the output carefully: it tells you the
current step number, prompt, skill docs, and past trajectories. If `next`
exits non-zero, the saga is complete or absent — do not invent work.

### 2. BEGIN — `agentrail begin`
Run immediately after reading `next` output. This transitions the step from
Pending to InProgress so the recorded history matches what actually
happened.

### 3. WORK
Do what the step prompt says. Do NOT ask the user "want me to proceed?" or
"shall I start?" — the step prompt IS your instruction. Execute it.

### 4. COMMIT
Commit your code changes with git BEFORE running `agentrail complete`.
The commit recorded into the step's `commits` field comes from `HEAD` at
the moment of `complete`, so the commit must land first.

### 5. COMPLETE — `agentrail complete`
```
agentrail complete --summary "what you accomplished" \
  --reward 1 \
  --actions "tools and approach used"
```
On failure: `--reward -1 --failure-mode "what went wrong"`.
On final step: add `--done`.

### 6. STOP
After `complete`, do NOT make further code changes. Anything after
`complete` is untracked and invisible to the next session. If you see more
work to do, it belongs in the NEXT step, not this one.

## Agentrail metadata discipline

When using agentrail, changes to `.agentrail/` files are first-class project
changes — the same as application source code. They must be committed, and
should be pushed before you hand off.

Before running `agentrail complete`:

1. `git status` — confirm `.agentrail/` files are tracked, not just present.
   Untracked files in `.agentrail/` mean the next session will not see them.
2. Stage and commit source changes and `.agentrail/` metadata together. The
   commit recorded into the step's `commits` field comes from `HEAD` at the
   moment of `agentrail complete`, so the commit must happen *first*.
3. Run `agentrail complete` after the commit lands.
4. Push the branch (or note the unpushed branch state in your handoff).

This is the most common agentrail failure mode: agents do the work, commit
the source, and forget the `.agentrail/` files. The result is a saga whose
recorded history disagrees with git history, which `agentrail audit` will
flag — but only after the damage is done.

### What's hand-editable in `.agentrail/`

Three categories of files live here, and the rules differ:

- **Append-only saga state** — `saga.toml`, `step.toml`, `plan.md`, session
  JSONLs under `sessions/`, trajectory JSONs under `trajectories/`, and
  anything under `.agentrail-archive/`. **Never hand-edit or delete these.**
  They are written by agentrail commands and represent the durable saga
  record; hand-editing desyncs the saga from git history and from prior
  session memory. A direct `rm` on untracked files is unrecoverable.
- **Regenerated state** — `instruction-lock.toml`. Don't hand-edit; it is
  rewritten on every `agentrail instructions apply`, so any local changes
  are overwritten silently.
- **User config** — `instruction-profile.toml`. This is normal user-edited
  config, like `.gitconfig` or a `package.json`. Hand-edit it freely, or
  use `agentrail instructions profile *` subcommands to mutate via
  commands (which validate field values and surface typos).

## Working a branch in parallel with another agent

If another agent is working this same repo on its own branch at the same
time, you are both writing into `.agentrail/`. Step numbers are
per-branch and *will* collide — you will both have a `003-` — so your
step directories land on identical paths and the merge conflicts. The
**slug** is the only part that can keep the two lanes apart.

Pick a lane prefix naming your slice of the work (`rtx5060`, `rtx3060`,
`api`, `ui`) and namespace your saga with it:

```bash
agentrail rename prefix <lane> --dry-run   # preview, changes nothing
agentrail rename prefix <lane>             # apply
git add -A .agentrail/                     # -A: a dir move is a delete + an add
git commit -m "saga: rename into <lane> lane"
```

`001-setup` becomes `001-<lane>-setup`, and the saga name is prefixed
too. Your directories no longer collide with the other agent's, so both
lanes survive the merge.

**Run it retroactively — that is what it is for.** You do not need to
decide on a lane before starting work. Renaming is not renumbering: step
numbers, statuses, completion timestamps, and recorded commits are all
preserved, so steps you have already completed keep their git-history
linkage and `agentrail audit` still matches them. Unlike `insert` and
`reorder`, which refuse to touch completed steps, `rename` is safe on
work that has already landed.

It is also **idempotent** — steps already carrying the prefix are
skipped — so just re-run it whenever you have added steps.

**Archive your lane before the merge.** Slug prefixing separates the step
directories, but both branches still have a single `saga.toml` and
overlapping step numbers, so merging two *live* lanes still conflicts.
When your lane is done:

```bash
agentrail complete --summary "..." --done
agentrail archive --reason "<lane> lane merged upstream"
```

Because the saga name was prefixed too, the archive directories are
distinct and the merge is completely conflict-free, with both lanes'
histories landing side by side.

Finer-grained forms: `agentrail rename step <N> <new-slug>` renames one
step, `agentrail rename saga <new-name>` renames only the saga.

## Branch handoff after `agentrail complete`

Once a feature branch is committed and `agentrail complete` has run,
signal that it is ready for review/merge by renaming it from
`feat/<slug>` to `pr/<slug>`:

```bash
git branch -m feat/<slug> pr/<slug>
```

The rename is a useful convention regardless of how this project
handles handoff:

- It distinguishes "in-progress work" from "awaiting review" in the
  output of `git branch`.
- Project-specific tooling (CI, release-engineer scans, automated PR
  creation) can key off the `pr/*` prefix.
- It keeps the branch name stable across the review cycle even if the
  feature slug evolves.

What happens after the rename depends on what push capability you
have. See `push-discipline.md` for how to detect capability before
trying.

- **You can push and use GitHub PRs.** Push the renamed branch and
  open the PR:
  ```bash
  git push -u origin pr/<slug>
  gh pr create
  ```
  (Or push and open the PR via the web UI.)
- **You cloned via HTTPS without push access to the upstream remote.**
  Typical when contributing to an open-source project you don't own:
  push the renamed branch to your fork instead, then open the PR
  pointing at upstream. `git remote -v` shows your remotes; add a
  fork remote with `git remote add fork <url>` if needed.
- **Your project has a project-specific handoff flow** (release
  engineer scanning for `pr/*` branches, automated PR creation, CI
  hooks). The rename IS the handoff signal. Look for site-specific
  guidance in CLAUDE.md / AGENTS.md outside the briefing markers — if
  present, follow that instead.

After the rename, do not continue committing to `pr/<slug>` — those
commits will not be in the PR. Start further work on a fresh branch
off the (eventually merged and pulled) base.

## Push discipline

When you push (typically after `branch-handoff` has renamed `feat/X`
to `pr/X` and you're publishing the PR branch), do it safely.

### Verify push capability before assuming it works

- `git remote get-url origin` — `git@…` (SSH) or `https://…` plus a
  configured credential helper is push-capable. A bare `https://…`
  with no helper usually is not (read-only mirror or fresh clone).
- `gh auth status` — if the project uses GitHub PRs and `gh` is not
  authenticated, `gh pr create` will fail.
- `git push --dry-run` — surfaces auth or branch-protection problems
  without changing remote state.

### If you cannot push (or push fails)

- Note the unpushed branch state explicitly in your `agentrail
  complete --summary` so the next session knows the work is local.
- Do NOT silently leave commits stranded on a local branch — the next
  agent will look at the remote and assume your work was lost.
- Do NOT retry the same `git push` in a loop. If the failure is a
  permission issue (no SSH key, no `gh` auth, sandboxed user), retries
  will not fix it. Surface the failure to the user.
- If this project has a project-specific handoff flow (release
  engineer scans for `pr/*` branches, queue files, CI hooks
  documented in CLAUDE.md / AGENTS.md outside the briefing markers),
  follow that instead of pushing — the branch rename from
  `branch-handoff.md` may already be sufficient.

### If the remote rejects a push

- For non-fast-forward errors on a personal branch, prefer
  `git pull --rebase` over `--force` unless the user has explicitly
  authorized force-push.
- Never force-push to a shared branch (`main`, release branches)
  without an explicit instruction.
- Never amend a commit that has already been pushed to a shared
  branch.

## Recovery: detecting and repairing saga/git drift

The saga is a record of git history. When the two diverge — agent forgets
to commit `.agentrail/`, a step is reverted, files are renamed by hand —
agentrail provides two recovery tools.

### Work done where the cursor never goes

A step finished in another lane, branch or repository stays `pending`
here, and once the cursor has passed it nothing brings the cursor back
(`agentrail status` lists such steps as **stranded**). Correct the record
with commands, never by hand-editing step.toml or by `reopen`-ing a
neighbor (that rewrites the neighbor's history):

```bash
agentrail close N --summary "..." --commit REF        # done in this repo
agentrail close N --summary "..." --elsewhere WHERE   # done elsewhere
agentrail edit N --prompt "..."          # a step not yet done, plan changed
agentrail reserve N --for OWNER          # someone else's: the cursor skips it
agentrail unreserve N                    # take it back
```

Reserve a step when you hand it off, before work starts, so it is never
stranded; `close` it when the owner reports it done.

### `agentrail audit`

Compares first-parent git history against saga steps and reports gaps.
Default output is a markdown report; `--emit-commands` prints a shell
script of `agentrail add` lines pre-seeded from commit subjects:

```bash
agentrail audit                    # human-readable report
agentrail audit --emit-commands    # draft script (review before running)
agentrail audit --since HEAD~50    # limit scope
```

The emitted script is a draft — slugs and prompts come from commit
subjects and usually need rewording. Review and edit before executing.

### `agentrail snapshot` (belt-and-suspenders)

Captures `.agentrail/` (and `.agentrail-archive/` if present) into a real
git commit under `refs/agentrail/snapshots/<timestamp>`. The blobs are
reachable, survive `git gc`, and can be restored with a normal git
command:

```bash
agentrail snapshot                 # take a snapshot now
agentrail snapshot --list          # list existing refs
git restore --source=<ref> -- .agentrail .agentrail-archive
```

Run a snapshot before risky agent operations or after creating files
you haven't yet staged. It does NOT replace normal git tracking — it is
a safety net for what is not yet committed.

## Git hygiene

- Never amend a commit that has already been pushed to a shared branch.
- Never use `--no-verify` to skip pre-commit hooks unless explicitly told to.
  If a hook fails, fix the underlying issue.
- Prefer naming files explicitly (`git add path/to/file`) over `git add -A`,
  to avoid sweeping in unintended files (secrets, local scratch, etc.).
- Resolve merge conflicts; do not discard changes by default.

## Project overview

reva-fork runs Ron Aaron's Reva Forth (`src/reva.f`, release 2011.2) on
a portable core: vx86, an IA-32-subset virtual machine in Rust, with
the original core's routines as Rust "gates". Hosts: the `reva` CLI,
a WebAssembly build for the browser, `reva-serve`, and a Tauri desktop
app. Version scheme `YYYY.MMDD.N` (see `components/host-base/crates/reva-version/src/version.rs`):
the day's version is set once (`.0`) and all of that day's work stays on
it; `.1`, `.2` ... only for another release shipped to `main` the same
day. Bump only when the user asks.

Read before working:

- `README.md`, `docs/README.md` -- what exists and the doc index
- `docs/design.md` -- architecture, deviations, roadmap
- `docs/parity.md` -- what runs, what does not, decisions
- `.agentrail/plan.md` -- the current saga

Layout: `components/<name>/` (one Cargo workspace each, crates in
`crates/`: macros, x86-types, x86-decode, x86-alu, x86-exec, x86, host-base, vfs, host,
core-parts, canvas, core, core-run, vlib, words-base, words-interp, words-dict,
words-os, words, vm, sqlite, cli-edit, cli-host, cli, web, serve, desktop; docs/design.md 3.13), `src/reva.f`, `lib/` (Forth libraries,
embedded into the VM), `examples/`, `docs/`, `tests/forth/` and
`work/reg-rs/` (goldens), `scripts/`, `justfile`. Everything builds into
`target/` at the root (`.cargo/config.toml`).

Code structure (the user's rules; docs/code-metrics.md): move out, up
and out, never combine; at most 4 modules per crate and 4 crates per
component, new components as needed; `lib.rs`/`mod.rs` hold only `mod`,
`use` and docs; pure functions; impls apart from structs; tests in
`tests/*_tests.rs`; boilerplate in macros, tables or build.rs; target
<=5 functions per module, <=25 lines per function.

## Lanes

Two agents work this repository:

- **local** (this Mac): sw-checklist conformance, bugs, features, and
  verification on macOS, which the cloud cannot run. Saga steps carry
  the `local-` prefix.
- **cloud**: CoSy, reva-fork's main user, here and in
  `ba-cosy-zip-fork`. It does not use this saga.

The local lane does not edit `ba-cosy-zip-fork`. Tell the user before
moving or renaming files the cloud lane edits (most of the core components: core, words, vlib, vm),
so the cloud lane can rebase.

## Invariants

- `src/reva.f` stays verbatim. What the port needs is inserted at boot
  by `components/host-base/crates/reva-embedded/src/embedded.rs`.
- Gate numbers (`components/core-parts/crates/reva-gate/src/gate.rs`) are append-only: saved
  images hold gate addresses.
- Refactors change no behaviour: tests, goldens and the web smoke test
  pass unchanged.
- A golden is a claim that the output is correct: review every diff
  before `reg-rs rebase`.
- No GPL-family code or crates (`scripts/license-check.sh`,
  `docs/licenses.md`).

## The gate

`just check` (`scripts/check.sh`) before every commit: fmt and
clippy `-D warnings` and tests in every component, the wasm build
and its node tests, the goldens on the release CLI, the license check,
and sw-checklist. `just check --fast` skips the desktop component.

The script lists goldens known to fail per OS and the most sw-checklist
FAILs allowed. Both may only shrink: lower them in the commit that
fixes something, never raise them.

Tools it needs on PATH: `reg-rs`, `sed-rs`, `sw-checklist`, `node`,
`just`; the `wasm32-unknown-unknown` target.

## Workflow

- One PR to `dev` per saga step, from `feat/<slug>`, renamed to
  `pr/<slug>` at handoff. `main` is updated from `dev` by the user.
- Commit messages: a subject line, a blank line, then what changed and
  why; end with the Co-Authored-By line.
- Every commit adds its line to `CHANGES.md` (newest first, under the
  day, Pacific time, a category from its header), in the same commit;
  saga records and merges too. A PR's merge line is added by the next
  commit on `dev`.
- Scripts run on macOS's bash 3.2 and BSD tools as well as Linux.

- [Shared Mac: don't steal focus](shared-mac-no-focus-stealing.md) — never raise windows; capture by window ID
- [Code structure rules](code-structure-rules.md) — move out not combine; <=4 modules/crate, <=4 crates/workspace; facade lib.rs; tests out of src
- [sw-checklist before features](checklist-before-features.md) — FAILs to 0, then features, then warnings last

`.agentrail/` directory) is the durable handoff between sessions — if your
work is not reflected there, the next session cannot see it.

Before reporting work as complete:

- Confirm the active step is reflected in `.agentrail/` and committed.
- Run the project's pre-commit gate (tests, lint, format) before
  `agentrail complete`, not after.
- If you discover unplanned work, prefer `agentrail insert` / `agentrail add`
  over silently doing it inside another step.

## CRITICAL: Agentrail session protocol (follow exactly)

Every session follows this sequence. Do not skip steps, do not reorder.

### 1. START — `agentrail next`
First thing in the session. Read the output carefully: it tells you the
current step number, prompt, skill docs, and past trajectories. If `next`
exits non-zero, the saga is complete or absent — do not invent work.

### 2. BEGIN — `agentrail begin`
Run immediately after reading `next` output. This transitions the step from
Pending to InProgress so the recorded history matches what actually
happened.

### 3. WORK
Do what the step prompt says. Do NOT ask the user "want me to proceed?" or
"shall I start?" — the step prompt IS your instruction. Execute it.

### 4. COMMIT
Commit your code changes with git BEFORE running `agentrail complete`.
The commit recorded into the step's `commits` field comes from `HEAD` at
the moment of `complete`, so the commit must land first.

### 5. COMPLETE — `agentrail complete`
```
agentrail complete --summary "what you accomplished" \
  --reward 1 \
  --actions "tools and approach used"
```
On failure: `--reward -1 --failure-mode "what went wrong"`.
On final step: add `--done`.

### 6. STOP
After `complete`, do NOT make further code changes. Anything after
`complete` is untracked and invisible to the next session. If you see more
work to do, it belongs in the NEXT step, not this one.

## Agentrail metadata discipline

When using agentrail, changes to `.agentrail/` files are first-class project
changes — the same as application source code. They must be committed, and
should be pushed before you hand off.

Before running `agentrail complete`:

1. `git status` — confirm `.agentrail/` files are tracked, not just present.
   Untracked files in `.agentrail/` mean the next session will not see them.
2. Stage and commit source changes and `.agentrail/` metadata together. The
   commit recorded into the step's `commits` field comes from `HEAD` at the
   moment of `agentrail complete`, so the commit must happen *first*.
3. Run `agentrail complete` after the commit lands.
4. Push the branch (or note the unpushed branch state in your handoff).

This is the most common agentrail failure mode: agents do the work, commit
the source, and forget the `.agentrail/` files. The result is a saga whose
recorded history disagrees with git history, which `agentrail audit` will
flag — but only after the damage is done.

### What's hand-editable in `.agentrail/`

Three categories of files live here, and the rules differ:

- **Append-only saga state** — `saga.toml`, `step.toml`, `plan.md`, session
  JSONLs under `sessions/`, trajectory JSONs under `trajectories/`, and
  anything under `.agentrail-archive/`. **Never hand-edit or delete these.**
  They are written by agentrail commands and represent the durable saga
  record; hand-editing desyncs the saga from git history and from prior
  session memory. A direct `rm` on untracked files is unrecoverable.
- **Regenerated state** — `instruction-lock.toml`. Don't hand-edit; it is
  rewritten on every `agentrail instructions apply`, so any local changes
  are overwritten silently.
- **User config** — `instruction-profile.toml`. This is normal user-edited
  config, like `.gitconfig` or a `package.json`. Hand-edit it freely, or
  use `agentrail instructions profile *` subcommands to mutate via
  commands (which validate field values and surface typos).

## Working a branch in parallel with another agent

If another agent is working this same repo on its own branch at the same
time, you are both writing into `.agentrail/`. Step numbers are
per-branch and *will* collide — you will both have a `003-` — so your
step directories land on identical paths and the merge conflicts. The
**slug** is the only part that can keep the two lanes apart.

Pick a lane prefix naming your slice of the work (`rtx5060`, `rtx3060`,
`api`, `ui`) and namespace your saga with it:

```bash
agentrail rename prefix <lane> --dry-run   # preview, changes nothing
agentrail rename prefix <lane>             # apply
git add -A .agentrail/                     # -A: a dir move is a delete + an add
git commit -m "saga: rename into <lane> lane"
```

`001-setup` becomes `001-<lane>-setup`, and the saga name is prefixed
too. Your directories no longer collide with the other agent's, so both
lanes survive the merge.

**Run it retroactively — that is what it is for.** You do not need to
decide on a lane before starting work. Renaming is not renumbering: step
numbers, statuses, completion timestamps, and recorded commits are all
preserved, so steps you have already completed keep their git-history
linkage and `agentrail audit` still matches them. Unlike `insert` and
`reorder`, which refuse to touch completed steps, `rename` is safe on
work that has already landed.

It is also **idempotent** — steps already carrying the prefix are
skipped — so just re-run it whenever you have added steps.

**Archive your lane before the merge.** Slug prefixing separates the step
directories, but both branches still have a single `saga.toml` and
overlapping step numbers, so merging two *live* lanes still conflicts.
When your lane is done:

```bash
agentrail complete --summary "..." --done
agentrail archive --reason "<lane> lane merged upstream"
```

Because the saga name was prefixed too, the archive directories are
distinct and the merge is completely conflict-free, with both lanes'
histories landing side by side.

Finer-grained forms: `agentrail rename step <N> <new-slug>` renames one
step, `agentrail rename saga <new-name>` renames only the saga.

## Branch handoff after `agentrail complete`

Once a feature branch is committed and `agentrail complete` has run,
signal that it is ready for review/merge by renaming it from
`feat/<slug>` to `pr/<slug>`:

```bash
git branch -m feat/<slug> pr/<slug>
```

The rename is a useful convention regardless of how this project
handles handoff:

- It distinguishes "in-progress work" from "awaiting review" in the
  output of `git branch`.
- Project-specific tooling (CI, release-engineer scans, automated PR
  creation) can key off the `pr/*` prefix.
- It keeps the branch name stable across the review cycle even if the
  feature slug evolves.

What happens after the rename depends on what push capability you
have. See `push-discipline.md` for how to detect capability before
trying.

- **You can push and use GitHub PRs.** Push the renamed branch and
  open the PR:
  ```bash
  git push -u origin pr/<slug>
  gh pr create
  ```
  (Or push and open the PR via the web UI.)
- **You cloned via HTTPS without push access to the upstream remote.**
  Typical when contributing to an open-source project you don't own:
  push the renamed branch to your fork instead, then open the PR
  pointing at upstream. `git remote -v` shows your remotes; add a
  fork remote with `git remote add fork <url>` if needed.
- **Your project has a project-specific handoff flow** (release
  engineer scanning for `pr/*` branches, automated PR creation, CI
  hooks). The rename IS the handoff signal. Look for site-specific
  guidance in CLAUDE.md / AGENTS.md outside the briefing markers — if
  present, follow that instead.

After the rename, do not continue committing to `pr/<slug>` — those
commits will not be in the PR. Start further work on a fresh branch
off the (eventually merged and pulled) base.

## Push discipline

When you push (typically after `branch-handoff` has renamed `feat/X`
to `pr/X` and you're publishing the PR branch), do it safely.

### Verify push capability before assuming it works

- `git remote get-url origin` — `git@…` (SSH) or `https://…` plus a
  configured credential helper is push-capable. A bare `https://…`
  with no helper usually is not (read-only mirror or fresh clone).
- `gh auth status` — if the project uses GitHub PRs and `gh` is not
  authenticated, `gh pr create` will fail.
- `git push --dry-run` — surfaces auth or branch-protection problems
  without changing remote state.

### If you cannot push (or push fails)

- Note the unpushed branch state explicitly in your `agentrail
  complete --summary` so the next session knows the work is local.
- Do NOT silently leave commits stranded on a local branch — the next
  agent will look at the remote and assume your work was lost.
- Do NOT retry the same `git push` in a loop. If the failure is a
  permission issue (no SSH key, no `gh` auth, sandboxed user), retries
  will not fix it. Surface the failure to the user.
- If this project has a project-specific handoff flow (release
  engineer scans for `pr/*` branches, queue files, CI hooks
  documented in CLAUDE.md / AGENTS.md outside the briefing markers),
  follow that instead of pushing — the branch rename from
  `branch-handoff.md` may already be sufficient.

### If the remote rejects a push

- For non-fast-forward errors on a personal branch, prefer
  `git pull --rebase` over `--force` unless the user has explicitly
  authorized force-push.
- Never force-push to a shared branch (`main`, release branches)
  without an explicit instruction.
- Never amend a commit that has already been pushed to a shared
  branch.

## Recovery: detecting and repairing saga/git drift

The saga is a record of git history. When the two diverge — agent forgets
to commit `.agentrail/`, a step is reverted, files are renamed by hand —
agentrail provides two recovery tools.

### Work done where the cursor never goes

A step finished in another lane, branch or repository stays `pending`
here, and once the cursor has passed it nothing brings the cursor back
(`agentrail status` lists such steps as **stranded**). Correct the record
with commands, never by hand-editing step.toml or by `reopen`-ing a
neighbor (that rewrites the neighbor's history):

```bash
agentrail close N --summary "..." --commit REF        # done in this repo
agentrail close N --summary "..." --elsewhere WHERE   # done elsewhere
agentrail edit N --prompt "..."          # a step not yet done, plan changed
agentrail reserve N --for OWNER          # someone else's: the cursor skips it
agentrail unreserve N                    # take it back
```

Reserve a step when you hand it off, before work starts, so it is never
stranded; `close` it when the owner reports it done.

### `agentrail audit`

Compares first-parent git history against saga steps and reports gaps.
Default output is a markdown report; `--emit-commands` prints a shell
script of `agentrail add` lines pre-seeded from commit subjects:

```bash
agentrail audit                    # human-readable report
agentrail audit --emit-commands    # draft script (review before running)
agentrail audit --since HEAD~50    # limit scope
```

The emitted script is a draft — slugs and prompts come from commit
subjects and usually need rewording. Review and edit before executing.

### `agentrail snapshot` (belt-and-suspenders)

Captures `.agentrail/` (and `.agentrail-archive/` if present) into a real
git commit under `refs/agentrail/snapshots/<timestamp>`. The blobs are
reachable, survive `git gc`, and can be restored with a normal git
command:

```bash
agentrail snapshot                 # take a snapshot now
agentrail snapshot --list          # list existing refs
git restore --source=<ref> -- .agentrail .agentrail-archive
```

Run a snapshot before risky agent operations or after creating files
you haven't yet staged. It does NOT replace normal git tracking — it is
a safety net for what is not yet committed.

## Git hygiene

- Never amend a commit that has already been pushed to a shared branch.
- Never use `--no-verify` to skip pre-commit hooks unless explicitly told to.
  If a hook fails, fix the underlying issue.
- Prefer naming files explicitly (`git add path/to/file`) over `git add -A`,
  to avoid sweeping in unintended files (secrets, local scratch, etc.).
- Resolve merge conflicts; do not discard changes by default.

- **Change stream:** `ui wait` host calls carry change lines. The page also gets the `reva_ui_take` export and the "tui" UI channel.
- **TUI in the page:** `www/tui.js` puts the TUI in the REPL column (`body.tui-on`), so the graphics pane stays visible.
- **IUP key codes** (IUP 3):
  - Modifier bits: SHIFT 0x10000000, CTRL 0x20000000, ALT, SYS.
  - Shift is dropped for Ctrl-letters, so `K_cZ` is the same with or without Shift; redo therefore uses Ctrl-Y.
- **Terminal UI** (crossterm 0.29):
  - Raw mode, alternate screen, mouse capture, bracketed paste.
  - Keyboard enhancement (DISAMBIGUATE_ESCAPE_CODES) where supported.
  - In raw mode `\n` decodes as Ctrl-J.
  - Ctrl-C closes the top dialog.
  - Suspends before the REPL prompts (`StdHost::read_line`), on Drop, and in a panic hook installed once.
- **Notebook library** `lib/ui/notebook`:
  - Words are `nb-*`, plus the public `notebook`.
  - Evaluation keys: F6, `K_cCR`, `K_cJ`. F1 shows help.
  - Text is saved to `notebook.txt`; `notebook.bak` is written at load.
- **Reva gotchas:**
  - `zt` writes a 0 in place, so text is copied before `attr`.
  - `callback` words run on their own stack; F6 is a plain word.
  - The loop is `repeat … while`; there is no `begin`.
  - `[']` is compile-only. `attr:` is a macro; `attr` is the function form.
  - `with~ ~ui` adds to the search order without making it current.
- **sed-rs:**
  - Reads stdin only (no `-i`) and has no address ranges.
  - It applies BRE conversion, so `\(` and `\+` are operators; use `[(]`, `[+]`, `[.]`.
  - zsh doesn't word-split `$var`; use `while read` loops.

| vim: ft=reva :
|
| ui/notebook -- a small notebook in the TUI (reva-fork; docs/ui-model.md)
|
|   needs ui/notebook  notebook
|
| Type a Forth line in the top pane and press F6 (fn+F6 on a Mac
| keyboard): the line under the cursor is evaluated, and what it prints,
| any error and the stack it leaves show in the lower pane.  Enter starts
| a new line, Tab moves between the panes and the Done button, Done or
| the x in the top border closes it.  It fills the window, and keeps the
| top pane's text in notebook.txt (in the current folder: the desktop
| app's, the browser's saved files), loaded when it opens.

push~

needs ui/gui

~
with~ ~ui

variable nb-text   variable nb-res   variable nb-status

| The line under the cursor of the top pane.
: nb-line ( -- a n )  nb-text @ caret-y? line-text? rot drop ;

| While a line is evaluated, what it prints goes to the lower pane.
| `attr` makes its strings C strings in place (a 0 after them), so what
| is typed (word names in the dictionary, for `words`) is copied first.
variable nb-old-emit   variable nb-old-type   variable nb-emit-pad
create nb-buf 256 allot
: nb-chunk ( a n -- )  >r nb-buf r@ move  nb-res @ nb-buf r> " INSERT" attr drop ;
: nb-type ( a n -- )
  repeat
    2dup 255 min dup >r nb-chunk
    swap r@ + swap r> -
  dup 0 > while 2drop ;
: nb-emit ( c -- )  nb-emit-pad c!  nb-emit-pad 1 nb-type ;
: nb-to-pane ( -- )
  ['] emit @ nb-old-emit !  ['] type @ nb-old-type !
  ['] nb-emit is emit  ['] nb-type is type ;
: nb-to-repl ( -- )  nb-old-emit @ is emit  nb-old-type @ is type ;

| What the line left on the stack, oldest first (what is above depth d0).
variable nb-d0
: nb-.new ( -- )
  depth nb-d0 @ - dup 0 > if dup 0 do dup i - pick . loop then drop ;

| The top pane's text is kept in notebook.txt: saved at every evaluation
| and when the notebook closes; what was there when it opened is copied
| to notebook.bak first, so a bad session can be undone.
: nb-file ( -- a n )  " notebook.txt" ;
: nb-write ( a n file n2 -- )  creat >r r@ write r> close ;
: nb-save ( -- )  nb-text @ getval rot drop  nb-file nb-write ;

| F6: evaluate the line; its output, any error and the stack below; then
| save.  A plain word, not a `callback` one: the TUI runs it on the data
| stack (as IUP called C callbacks) and puts the stack back afterwards, so
| words like `help` and `.s` work as at the REPL.
: nb-f6
  nb-res @ " " setval drop
  depth nb-d0 !
  nb-to-pane
  nb-line ['] eval catch ?dup if ." error " . cr then
  cr ." stack: " nb-.new
  nb-to-repl
  nb-res @ " 1,1" " CARET" attr drop
  nb-status @ " evaluated" title drop
  nb-save
  gui-default ;

| Ctrl-X Ctrl-E: evaluate, as in Emacs (and the REPLs); Ctrl-E alone is
| still the end of the line, and any other key after Ctrl-X is itself.
variable nb-prefix
: nb-cx ( -- n )  nb-prefix on gui-ignore ;
: nb-ce ( -- n )  nb-prefix @ if nb-prefix off nb-f6 else gui-default then ;
: nb-any ( -- n )  nb-prefix off gui-default ;

| F1: what the keys do, in the lower pane.
: nb-.help ( -- )
  ." Ctrl-J, Cmd-Enter or F6 (fn+F6 on a Mac): evaluate the line (in a" cr
  ."        terminal Ctrl-J or F6: it gets no Cmd-Enter);" cr
  ."        what it prints, any error and the stack it leaves show here" cr
  ." Enter  a new line; arrows, Home, End, Ctrl-A, Ctrl-E, Ctrl-K edit" cr
  ." Cmd-V  paste (Ctrl-V elsewhere)     Tab  the next pane or button" cr
  ." Cmd-Z  undo (Ctrl-Z elsewhere)      Ctrl-Y  redo" cr
  ." Done   or the x in the top border: close.  The text is saved in" cr
  ."        notebook.txt at each evaluation and on closing; notebook.bak" cr
  ."        holds what it was when the notebook opened" cr
  ." Forth needs a space between words: 6 7 *  not  6 7*" ;
: nb-f1
  nb-res @ " " setval drop
  nb-to-pane nb-.help nb-to-repl
  nb-res @ " 1,1" " CARET" attr drop
  gui-default ;

: nb-dialog ( -- dialog )
  dialog[
    " Ctrl-J or F6 evaluates the line  -  F1 help  -  Done closes" label[ expand-horizontal dup nb-status ! ]w
    editbox[ expand
      ['] nb-f6 z" K_F6" set-callback
      ['] nb-f6 z" K_cCR" set-callback
      ['] nb-f6 z" K_cJ" set-callback
      ['] nb-f1 z" K_F1" set-callback
      dup nb-text ! ]w
    editbox[ " x64" size expand-horizontal dup nb-res ! ]w
    hbox[ " Done" button[ { gui-close } action ]w ]w
  ]d " FULLxFULL" size " Reva notebook" title ;

| A first notebook (no notebook.txt yet) starts with lines to try.
: nb-line+ ( a n -- )  nb-text @ -rot " APPEND" attr drop ;
: nb-examples ( -- )
  " | Put the cursor on a line and press Ctrl-J (or F6).  F1: help." nb-line+
  " 2 3 +" nb-line+
  " 6 7 * dup . 1+" nb-line+
  " : sq dup * ;  7 sq" nb-line+
  " : tens  10 0 do i 10 * . loop ;  tens" nb-line+
  " words" nb-line+
  nb-text @ " 2,1" " CARET" attr drop ;
| Load notebook.txt (copied to notebook.bak first), or the examples.
: nb-load ( -- )
  nb-file slurp dup 0if 2drop nb-examples ;then
  2dup " notebook.bak" nb-write  nb-text @ -rot setval drop ;

| Open the notebook; it returns when the notebook is closed.
: notebook ( -- )  nb-dialog nb-load show gui-main-loop nb-save destroy ;

pop~

|||

def: notebook
ctx: ~
stack: --
desc: =
Opens a small notebook in the TUI: type Forth lines in the top pane, F6
evaluates the line under the cursor and shows what it printed, any error
and the stack it left in the lower pane.  Done or the close box closes it;
its text is kept in notebook.txt.
=

# Claude in Chrome browser automation
