Every session follows this sequence. Do not skip steps, do not reorder.

### 1. START — `agentrail next`
First thing in the session. Read the output carefully: it tells you the
current step number, prompt, skill docs, and past trajectories. If `next`
exits non-zero, the saga is complete or absent — do not invent work.

### 2. BEGIN — `agentrail begin`
Run immediately after reading `next` output. This transitions the step from
Pending to InProgress so the recorded history matches what actually
happened.

### 3. WORK
Do what the step prompt says. Do NOT ask the user "want me to proceed?" or
"shall I start?" — the step prompt IS your instruction. Execute it.

### 4. COMMIT
Commit your code changes with git BEFORE running `agentrail complete`.
The commit recorded into the step's `commits` field comes from `HEAD` at
the moment of `complete`, so the commit must land first.

### 5. COMPLETE — `agentrail complete`
```
agentrail complete --summary "what you accomplished" \
  --reward 1 \
  --actions "tools and approach used"
```
On failure: `--reward -1 --failure-mode "what went wrong"`.
On final step: add `--done`.

### 6. STOP
After `complete`, do NOT make further code changes. Anything after
`complete` is untracked and invisible to the next session. If you see more
work to do, it belongs in the NEXT step, not this one.

## Agentrail metadata discipline

When using agentrail, changes to `.agentrail/` files are first-class project
changes — the same as application source code. They must be committed, and
should be pushed before you hand off.

Before running `agentrail complete`:

1. `git status` — confirm `.agentrail/` files are tracked, not just present.
   Untracked files in `.agentrail/` mean the next session will not see them.
2. Stage and commit source changes and `.agentrail/` metadata together. The
   commit recorded into the step's `commits` field comes from `HEAD` at the
   moment of `agentrail complete`, so the commit must happen *first*.
3. Run `agentrail complete` after the commit lands.
4. Push the branch (or note the unpushed branch state in your handoff).

the source, and forget the `.agentrail/` files. The result is a saga whose
recorded history disagrees with git history, which `agentrail audit` will
flag — but only after the damage is done.

- **Append-only saga state** — `saga.toml`, `step.toml`, `plan.md`, session

  anything under `.agentrail-archive/`. **Never hand-edit or delete these.**

- **Regenerated state** — `instruction-lock.toml`. Don't hand-edit; it is
  rewritten on every `agentrail instructions apply`, so any local changes
  are overwritten silently.
- **User config** — `instruction-profile.toml`. This is normal user-edited

step directories land on identical paths and the merge conflicts. The
**slug** is the only part that can keep the two lanes apart.


content.content:
Insert a new pending step at a chosen position, shifting later steps up

Use when a bug or unplanned task needs to slot in before existing pending work. The new step lands at position `after + 1`; every pending/in-progress step with a number greater than `after` shifts up by one (step.toml `number` and the on-disk `NNN-slug` directory name are both updated). The operation is refused if any step that would shift is already `Completed`, since completed steps anchor git-tracked history.

Pass `--after 0` to prepend at position 1 (only works if step 1 is pending).

Cursor semantic (preemption): if the new step lands at or before the current cursor, focus follows the new arrival — the inserted step becomes `current_step` and the previously focused step is pushed to `current_step + 1`. This matches the "drop in a blocker" use case. If the new step lands behind the cursor, focus is unchanged and the new step is queued as future work.

| a new line, Tab moves between the panes and the Done button, Done or
| the x in the top border closes it.  It fills the window, and keeps the
| top pane's text in notebook.txt (in the current folder: the desktop
| app's, the browser's saved files), loaded when it opens.

push~

needs ui/gui

~
with~ ~ui

variable nb-text   variable nb-res   variable nb-status

| The line under the cursor of the top pane.
: nb-line ( -- a n )  nb-text @ caret-y? line-text? rot drop ;

| While a line is evaluated, what it prints goes to the lower pane.
| `attr` makes its strings C strings in place (a 0 after them), so what
| is typed (word names in the dictionary, for `words`) is copied first.
variable nb-old-emit   variable nb-old-type   variable nb-emit-pad
create nb-buf 256 allot
: nb-chunk ( a n -- )  >r nb-buf r@ move  nb-res @ nb-buf r> " INSERT" attr drop ;
: nb-type ( a n -- )
  repeat
    2dup 255 min dup >r nb-chunk
    swap r@ + swap r> -
  dup 0 > while 2drop ;
: nb-emit ( c -- )  nb-emit-pad c!  nb-emit-pad 1 nb-type ;
: nb-to-pane ( -- )
  ['] emit @ nb-old-emit !  ['] type @ nb-old-type !
  ['] nb-emit is emit  ['] nb-type is type ;
: nb-to-repl ( -- )  nb-old-emit @ is emit  nb-old-type @ is type ;

| What the line left on the stack, oldest first (what is above depth d0).
variable nb-d0
: nb-.new ( -- )
  depth nb-d0 @ - dup 0 > if dup 0 do dup i - pick . loop then drop ;

| The top pane's text is kept in notebook.txt: saved at every evaluation
| and when the notebook closes; what was there when it opened is copied
| to notebook.bak first, so a bad session can be undone.
: nb-file ( -- a n )  " notebook.txt" ;
: nb-write ( a n file n2 -- )  creat >r r@ write r> close ;
: nb-save ( -- )  nb-text @ getval rot drop  nb-file nb-write ;

| F6: evaluate the line; its output, any error and the stack below; then
| save.  A plain word, not a `callback` one: the TUI runs it on the data
| stack (as IUP called C callbacks) and puts the stack back afterwards, so
| words like `help` and `.s` work as at the REPL.
: nb-f6
  nb-res @ " " setval drop
  depth nb-d0 !
  nb-to-pane
  nb-line ['] eval catch ?dup if ." error " . cr then
  cr ." stack: " nb-.new
  nb-to-repl
  nb-res @ " 1,1" " CARET" attr drop
  nb-status @ " evaluated" title drop
  nb-save
  gui-default ;

| Ctrl-X Ctrl-E: evaluate, as in Emacs (and the REPLs); Ctrl-E alone is
| still the end of the line, and any other key after Ctrl-X is itself.
variable nb-prefix
: nb-cx ( -- n )  nb-prefix on gui-ignore ;
: nb-ce ( -- n )  nb-prefix @ if nb-prefix off nb-f6 else gui-default then ;
: nb-any ( -- n )  nb-prefix off gui-default ;

| F1: what the keys do, in the lower pane.
: nb-.help ( -- )
  ." Ctrl-J, Cmd-Enter or F6 (fn+F6 on a Mac): evaluate the line (in a" cr
  ."        terminal Ctrl-J or F6: it gets no Cmd-Enter);" cr
  ."        what it prints, any error and the stack it leaves show here" cr
  ." Enter  a new line; arrows, Home, End, Ctrl-A, Ctrl-E, Ctrl-K edit" cr
  ." Cmd-V  paste (Ctrl-V elsewhere)     Tab  the next pane or button" cr
  ." Cmd-Z  undo (Ctrl-Z elsewhere)      Ctrl-Y  redo" cr
  ." Done   or the x in the top border: close.  The text is saved in" cr
  ."        notebook.txt at each evaluation and on closing; notebook.bak" cr
  ."        holds what it was when the notebook opened" cr
  ." Forth needs a space between words: 6 7 *  not  6 7*" ;
: nb-f1
  nb-res @ " " setval drop
  nb-to-pane nb-.help nb-to-repl
  nb-res @ " 1,1" " CARET" attr drop
  gui-default ;

: nb-dialog ( -- dialog )
  dialog[
    " Ctrl-J or F6 evaluates the line  -  F1 help  -  Done closes" label[ expand-horizontal dup nb-status ! ]w
    editbox[ expand
      ['] nb-f6 z" K_F6" set-callback
      ['] nb-f6 z" K_cCR" set-callback
      ['] nb-f6 z" K_cJ" set-callback
      ['] nb-f1 z" K_F1" set-callback
      dup nb-text ! ]w
    editbox[ " x64" size expand-horizontal dup nb-res ! ]w
    hbox[ " Done" button[ { gui-close } action ]w ]w
  ]d " FULLxFULL" size " Reva notebook" title ;

| A first notebook (no notebook.txt yet) starts with lines to try.
: nb-line+ ( a n -- )  nb-text @ -rot " APPEND" attr drop ;
: nb-examples ( -- )
  " | Put the cursor on a line and press Ctrl-J (or F6).  F1: help." nb-line+
  " 2 3 +" nb-line+
  " 6 7 * dup . 1+" nb-line+
  " : sq dup * ;  7 sq" nb-line+
  " : tens  10 0 do i 10 * . loop ;  tens" nb-line+
  " words" nb-line+
  nb-text @ " 2,1" " CARET" attr drop ;
| Load notebook.txt (copied to notebook.bak first), or the examples.
: nb-load ( -- )
  nb-file slurp dup 0if 2drop nb-examples ;then
  2dup " notebook.bak" nb-write  nb-text @ -rot setval drop ;

| Open the notebook; it returns when the notebook is closed.
: notebook ( -- )  nb-dialog nb-load show gui-main-loop nb-save destroy ;

pop~

| Ctrl-X, then Ctrl-E | evaluate the line, like Ctrl-J or F6 |
| Ctrl-X, then any other key | that key does its usual thing |

So you don't need it unless you want the Emacs habit. Ctrl-J and fn-F6 still evaluate, and they're simpler.

There is one place where Ctrl-X really did have two meanings. In the browser on Linux and Windows, Ctrl-X is the system's **cut**:
- **REPL input line:** the chord now takes Ctrl-X, so cut there needs Shift-Delete or the menu. That matches how the line already treats Ctrl-A, Ctrl-K and Ctrl-W as Emacs keys. On a Mac nothing changes, because cut is Cmd-X.
- **Notebook page:** the browser keeps Cmd-X for cut, but Ctrl-X now goes to the notebook for the chord.

If you'd rather keep the system's cut on Linux, I can drop the chord from the browser and keep it only in the CLI and the notebook.

The full golden run is still going. I'll review the two notebook golden diffs when it finishes.

toolUseResult.originalFile:
| vim: ft=reva :
|
| ui/notebook -- a small notebook in the TUI (reva-fork; docs/ui-model.md)
|
|   needs ui/notebook  notebook
|
| Type a Forth line in the top pane and press F6 (fn+F6 on a Mac
| keyboard): the line under the cursor is evaluated, and what it prints,
| any error and the stack it leaves show in the lower pane.  Enter starts
| a new line, Tab moves between the panes and the Done button, Done or
| the x in the top border closes it.  It fills the window, and keeps the
| top pane's text in notebook.txt (in the current folder: the desktop
| app's, the browser's saved files), loaded when it opens.

push~

needs ui/gui

~
with~ ~ui

variable nb-text   variable nb-res   variable nb-status

| The line under the cursor of the top pane.
: nb-line ( -- a n )  nb-text @ caret-y? line-text? rot drop ;

| While a line is evaluated, what it prints goes to the lower pane.
| `attr` makes its strings C strings in place (a 0 after them), so what
| is typed (word names in the dictionary, for `words`) is copied first.
variable nb-old-emit   variable nb-old-type   variable nb-emit-pad
create nb-buf 256 allot
: nb-chunk ( a n -- )  >r nb-buf r@ move  nb-res @ nb-buf r> " INSERT" attr drop ;
: nb-type ( a n -- )
  repeat
    2dup 255 min dup >r nb-chunk
    swap r@ + swap r> -
  dup 0 > while 2drop ;
: nb-emit ( c -- )  nb-emit-pad c!  nb-emit-pad 1 nb-type ;
: nb-to-pane ( -- )
  ['] emit @ nb-old-emit !  ['] type @ nb-old-type !
  ['] nb-emit is emit  ['] nb-type is type ;
: nb-to-repl ( -- )  nb-old-emit @ is emit  nb-old-type @ is type ;

| What the line left on the stack, oldest first (what is above depth d0).
variable nb-d0
: nb-.new ( -- )
  depth nb-d0 @ - dup 0 > if dup 0 do dup i - pick . loop then drop ;

| The top pane's text is kept in notebook.txt: saved at every evaluation
| and when the notebook closes; what was there when it opened is copied
| to notebook.bak first, so a bad session can be undone.
: nb-file ( -- a n )  " notebook.txt" ;
: nb-write ( a n file n2 -- )  creat >r r@ write r> close ;
: nb-save ( -- )  nb-text @ getval rot drop  nb-file nb-write ;

| F6: evaluate the line; its output, any error and the stack below; then
| save.  A plain word, not a `callback` one: the TUI runs it on the data
| stack (as IUP called C callbacks) and puts the stack back afterwards, so
| words like `help` and `.s` work as at the REPL.
: nb-f6
  nb-res @ " " setval drop
  depth nb-d0 !
  nb-to-pane
  nb-line ['] eval catch ?dup if ." error " . cr then
  cr ." stack: " nb-.new
  nb-to-repl
  nb-res @ " 1,1" " CARET" attr drop
  nb-status @ " evaluated" title drop
  nb-save
  gui-default ;

| Ctrl-X Ctrl-E: evaluate, as in Emacs (and the REPLs); Ctrl-E alone is
| still the end of the line, and any other key after Ctrl-X is itself.
variable nb-prefix
: nb-cx ( -- n )  nb-prefix on gui-ignore ;
: nb-ce ( -- n )  nb-prefix @ if nb-prefix off nb-f6 else gui-default then ;
: nb-any ( -- n )  nb-prefix off gui-default ;

| F1: what the keys do, in the lower pane.
: nb-.help ( -- )
  ." Ctrl-J, Ctrl-X Ctrl-E, Cmd-Enter or F6 (fn+F6 on a Mac): evaluate" cr
  ."        the line (a terminal gets no Cmd-Enter);" cr
  ."        what it prints, any error and the stack it leaves show here" cr
  ." Enter  a new line; arrows, Home, End, Ctrl-A, Ctrl-E, Ctrl-K edit" cr
  ." Cmd-V  paste (Ctrl-V elsewhere)     Tab  the next pane or button" cr
  ." Cmd-Z  undo (Ctrl-Z elsewhere)      Ctrl-Y  redo" cr
  ." Done   or the x in the top border: close.  The text is saved in" cr
  ."        notebook.txt at each evaluation and on closing; notebook.bak" cr
  ."        holds what it was when the notebook opened" cr
  ." Forth needs a space between words: 6 7 *  not  6 7*" ;
: nb-f1
  nb-res @ " " setval drop
  nb-to-pane nb-.help nb-to-repl
  nb-res @ " 1,1" " CARET" attr drop
  gui-default ;

: nb-dialog ( -- dialog )
  dialog[
    " Ctrl-J or F6 evaluates the line  -  F1 help  -  Done closes" label[ expand-horizontal dup nb-status ! ]w
    editbox[ expand
      ['] nb-f6 z" K_F6" set-callback
      ['] nb-f6 z" K_cCR" set-callback
      ['] nb-f6 z" K_cJ" set-callback
      ['] nb-cx z" K_cX" set-callback
      ['] nb-ce z" K_cE" set-callback
      ['] nb-any z" K_ANY" set-callback
      ['] nb-f1 z" K_F1" set-callback
      dup nb-text ! ]w
    editbox[ " x64" size expand-horizontal dup nb-res ! ]w
    hbox[ " Done" button[ { gui-close } action ]w ]w
  ]d " FULLxFULL" size " Reva notebook" title ;

| A first notebook (no notebook.txt yet) starts with lines to try.
: nb-line+ ( a n -- )  nb-text @ -rot " APPEND" attr drop ;
: nb-examples ( -- )
  " | Put the cursor on a line and press Ctrl-J (or F6).  F1: help." nb-line+
  " 2 3 +" nb-line+
  " 6 7 * dup . 1+" nb-line+
  " : sq dup * ;  7 sq" nb-line+
  " : tens  10 0 do i 10 * . loop ;  tens" nb-line+
  " words" nb-line+
  nb-text @ " 2,1" " CARET" attr drop ;
| Load notebook.txt (copied to notebook.bak first), or the examples.
: nb-load ( -- )
  nb-file slurp dup 0if 2drop nb-examples ;then
  2dup " notebook.bak" nb-write  nb-text @ -rot setval drop ;

| Open the notebook; it returns when the notebook is closed.
: notebook ( -- )  nb-dialog nb-load show gui-main-loop nb-save destroy ;

pop~

|||

## The notebook and IUP dialogs

`needs ui/notebook notebook` opens the TUI notebook on the page
([ui-model.md](ui-model.md#the-tui)), as do other IUP programs' dialogs.
While a dialog is shown, the TUI takes the place of the REPL's output and
input line in the REPL column; the graphics pane stays beside it in the
split view (`?canvas=split`, the live demo's default), so a notebook line

notebook's text is kept in `notebook.txt`, which the page saves with its
other files in local storage (`reva:fs:/notebook.txt`), so it is there
again after a reload. Try it:
<http://localhost:8000/?canvas=split&eval=needs%20ui/notebook%20notebook>.

# The REPL: history and line editing

Every Reva REPL keeps a history of the lines typed at `ok>` and edits the
current line with Emacs keys (the readline/bash defaults).  This page is
the key table both front ends follow.

| Keys | What it does |
|------|--------------|
| Up / Down, Ctrl-P / Ctrl-N | previous / next history entry (Down past the newest brings back the line you were typing) |
| Ctrl-R / Ctrl-S | search history backward / forward; type to narrow, press again for the next match |
| Enter (while searching) | run the match |
| Esc, Ctrl-G, Ctrl-C (while searching) | give up, put the line back |
| any other key (while searching) | keep the match on the line, then do that key's usual thing |
| Ctrl-A / Ctrl-E | start / end of line |
| Ctrl-B / Ctrl-F | back / forward a character |
| Alt-B / Alt-F | back / forward a word |
| Ctrl-D, Ctrl-H | delete the character under / before the cursor |
| Ctrl-K / Ctrl-U | kill to end / start of line |
| Ctrl-W, Alt-Backspace | kill the word before the cursor |
| Alt-D | kill the word after the cursor |
| Ctrl-Y | yank (paste) the last kill |
| Ctrl-T | transpose characters |
| Ctrl-L | clear the screen (CLI only) |
| Ctrl-C | CLI: drop the line, new prompt (while a word runs: ends `reva`, as before); web: stop the running word |
| Ctrl-D on an empty line | CLI: end of input (`reva` exits 0) |

## Command line: `reva`

* **Only at a terminal.**  When stdin is a terminal, `reva` reads each line
  through its own small editor (components cli-edit and cli-host: reva-lineedit, reva-term; `scripts/pty-lineedit.py` drives it at a pseudo-terminal in the regression suite).
  Piped or redirected input is read as before, byte for byte, so scripts
  and the reg-rs goldens see no change.
* **History file:** `$REVA_HISTORY` if set (set it empty for no file),
  else `~/.reva_history` (`%USERPROFILE%\.reva_history` on Windows).
  Each line is appended as it is entered, so history survives `bye`,
  `restart`, a crash and `run-cosy`'s restart loop.  1000 entries are kept;
  the file is trimmed when it grows past 2000.  CoSy's `run-cosy` uses
  `~/.cosy_history`, so CoSy and plain Reva keep separate histories.
* **Off switches:** `reva --no-edit`, or `TERM=dumb`, reads plain lines
  (the terminal's own editing only).  If the terminal cannot be put in raw
  mode (for example Git Bash's mintty), `reva` falls back to plain lines
  by itself.
* Long lines scroll sideways on one row instead of wrapping.
* **Colour listings:** `pp FILE` (after `needs highlight/core`) lists
  source in colour; see [highlight.md](highlight.md) and `reva --color`.
* If the terminal is ever left in a strange state, `stty sane` (Unix)

# The REPL: history and line editing

Every Reva REPL keeps a history of the lines typed at `ok>` and edits the
current line with Emacs keys (the readline/bash defaults).  This page is
the key table both front ends follow.

| Keys | What it does |
|------|--------------|
| Up / Down, Ctrl-P / Ctrl-N | previous / next history entry (Down past the newest brings back the line you were typing) |
| Ctrl-R / Ctrl-S | search history backward / forward; type to narrow, press again for the next match |
| Enter (while searching) | run the match |
| Esc, Ctrl-G, Ctrl-C (while searching) | give up, put the line back |
| any other key (while searching) | keep the match on the line, then do that key's usual thing |
| Ctrl-A / Ctrl-E | start / end of line |
| Ctrl-B / Ctrl-F | back / forward a character |
| Alt-B / Alt-F | back / forward a word |
| Ctrl-D, Ctrl-H | delete the character under / before the cursor |
| Ctrl-K / Ctrl-U | kill to end / start of line |
| Ctrl-W, Alt-Backspace | kill the word before the cursor |
| Alt-D | kill the word after the cursor |
| Ctrl-Y | yank (paste) the last kill |
| Ctrl-T | transpose characters |
| Ctrl-X Ctrl-E | run the line, as Enter does (Emacs's chord; it evaluates a line in the notebook too); any other key after Ctrl-X is itself |
| Ctrl-L | clear the screen (CLI only) |

git commit -q -F - <<'EOF'
The TUI in the CLI's terminal; notebook keys, undo, autosave

Step local-ui-terminal. At an interactive terminal the CLI draws IUP
programs' dialogs (the notebook included) full screen with crossterm:
new crate reva-ui-term in component iup, the same cells as the browser
and the desktop app, only changed cells redrawn. Keys, clicks, pastes
and resizes go back as events; Ctrl-C closes the dialog on top; the
REPL gets the terminal back before it prompts, at exit and on a panic.

At the user's requests, also:
- Ctrl-J and Ctrl-X Ctrl-E evaluate a notebook line (no Cmd-Enter
  reaches a terminal); the chord runs the line in the CLI's and the
  page's REPL too. In the page Ctrl-X goes to the program; Cmd-X cuts.
- Undo (Ctrl-Z) and redo (Ctrl-Y) in text elements (reva-ui-text).
- The notebook saves notebook.txt at each evaluation; notebook.bak
  keeps what it held at opening.
- A paste's line breaks are one Enter each (shared reva-ui-base
  pasted(); terminals send \r).
- Notebook goldens run in a temp dir (scripts/in-tempdir.sh).
- Step local-cli-drawings queued as step 34.

Goldens reviewed: the notebook's new key text and shorter help, the
help entry, and the CLI's new refusal message in parity-examples.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
EOF

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# License gate: keep copyleft code and unreviewed binaries out of the tree.
#
#   scripts/license-check.sh          (checks the whole repository)
#
# 1. No tracked file may carry GPL, LGPL or AGPL license text.
# 2. Every tracked binary (ELF, PE, Mach-O, object file, archive) must be on
#    the reviewed list below, with its license.  Each listed path must also
#    appear in docs/licenses.md, so the inventory and the gate cannot drift.
# 3. If cargo-deny is installed, `cargo deny check licenses` must pass in
#    each Cargo workspace, components/*/ (deny.toml holds the list).  Without
#    it, a note is printed.
#
# Only git-tracked files are checked, so build output never trips the gate.
# Exit 1 on any failure.  Works with the bash 3.2 that macOS ships.
set -euo pipefail
cd "$(dirname "$0")/.."
status=0
fail() { echo "license-check: $*"; status=1; }

# Reviewed binaries: path, then license (see docs/licenses.md for the source
# of each judgement).  Adding a binary means reviewing it and adding it here.
# Read with `read -d ''`, not `$(cat <<EOF ...)`: bash 3.2 (macOS /bin/bash)
# mis-parses a here-document inside `$( )` when the text has an apostrophe.
read -r -d '' reviewed <<'EOF' || true
legacy/bin/lin/build                    Reva (public domain)
legacy/bin/lin/core                     Reva (public domain)
legacy/bin/lin/reva                     Reva (public domain)
legacy/bin/lin/libimath.so              IMath (MIT)
legacy/bin/lin/libiupall.so             IUP (MIT)
legacy/bin/lin/shabal.so                Reva scratch, Ron Aaron (presumed public domain)
legacy/bin/mac/build                    Reva (public domain), UPX-packed
legacy/bin/mac/core                     Reva (public domain), UPX-packed
legacy/bin/mac/reva                     Reva (public domain), UPX-packed
legacy/bin/mac/libcd.dylib              CD (MIT)
legacy/bin/mac/libcdcontextplus.dylib   CD (MIT)
legacy/bin/mac/libcdgdk.dylib           CD (MIT); links the system GDK
legacy/bin/mac/libfreetype.dylib        FreeType (FTL, chosen from FTL/GPL-2.0)
legacy/bin/mac/libimath.dylib           IMath (MIT)
legacy/bin/mac/libiup.dylib             IUP (MIT)
            }
            let depth = (S0 - esi) / 4;
            let mut v: Vec<u32> = (1..depth)
                .map(|k| self.mem.read_u32(S0 - 4 - 4 * k).unwrap_or(0))
                .collect();
            v.push(self.cpu.r[EAX as usize]);
            v
        }

        /// The turtle and its drawing (reva-vlib's `turtle`), for a host to
        /// stream or save.
        fn canvas(&mut self) -> &mut Canvas {
            &mut self.canvas
        }

        /// The exit code, once halted.
        fn halted(&self) -> Option<i32> {
            self.halted
        }
    }
}

content.content:
reg-rs (regress) - A CLI for regression testing

reg-rs captures command output and exit codes as baseline 'golden' results,
then compares subsequent runs against these baselines to detect regressions.

Tests are stored in ~/.local/reg-rs/ by default (override with REG_RS_DATA_DIR).

WORKFLOW:
  1. Create a test:   reg-rs create -t my_test -c 'my_command'
  2. Run the test:    reg-rs run -p my_test
  3. View results:    reg-rs report -p my_test -v

AI CODING AGENT INSTRUCTIONS:
  This tool is designed to be used by AI coding agents to ensure system integrity.
  1. Use 'reg-rs create' to establish baselines for new features.
  2. Use 'reg-rs run' to verify that changes haven't introduced regressions.
  3. Use 'reg-rs status' for real-time monitoring of long-running test suites.
  4. Always address failures before committing code.

Usage: reg-rs [OPTIONS] <COMMAND>

Commands:
  create    Create a new test
  analyze   Analyze a test failure using AI
  show      Shows detailed information about a test
  list      Lists all tests matching a pattern
  complete  Outputs test names for shell tab-completion
  reset     Clears latest run results
  migrate   Converts existing .tdb test databases to .rgt format
  rebase    Accepts the latest test output as new baseline
Creates a new test by executing a command and storing its output.

The command's stdout, stderr, and exit code are captured and stored in a
SQLite database file. This becomes the baseline for future regression tests.

Use --command to specify an explicit shell command, or --describe to have
an AI generate the command from a natural language description.
Requires ANTHROPIC_API_KEY environment variable when using --describe.

EXAMPLES:
  reg-rs create -t pwd_test -c 'pwd'
  reg-rs create -t version -c 'git --version'
  reg-rs c -t ls_test -c 'ls -la'     # using alias
  reg-rs create -t status -D 'show git status of current directory'

Usage: reg-rs create [OPTIONS] --test <TEST>

Options:
  -t, --test <TEST>
          Test name

  -c, --command <COMMAND>
          Shell command to execute

  -D, --describe <DESCRIBE>
          AI-generated command description

  -C, --context <CONTEXT>
          Context command for AI generation

# What reva-fork needs from sed-rs

Requests from using [sed-rs](https://github.com/sw-cli-tools/sed-rs) to
edit this repository's files (2026-11-01), most valuable first. Each has
the case that hit it and what would have fixed it.

Today an in-place edit is written as the user's undoable pattern:

```bash
mv file file.orig && sed-rs -e 's/old/new/' < file.orig > file
# wrong? mv file.orig file      right? rm file.orig
```

## 1. In-place editing with a backup: `-i[SUFFIX]`

```bash
sed-rs -i.orig -e 's/old/new/' file      # file.orig keeps the original
sed-rs -i -e 's/old/new/' a.rs b.rs      # several files, no backup
```

- Write the result to a temporary file in the same directory, then rename
  it over the original, so a reader never sees a half-written file.
- If the script does not parse, or any error occurs, leave every file
  untouched and exit non-zero before writing anything.
- Keep the file's permissions.

**Why:** a script that sed-rs rejected ("address ranges are not
supported") still left `> CHANGES.md` truncating the file, and the
command went on to commit an empty CHANGES.md. With `-i`, a failed
script changes nothing.

## 2. Address ranges, and "first match only"

```bash
sed-rs -e '0,/^## 2026-11-01$/s//## 2026-11-01\n\n- new line/'   # first match only
sed-rs -e '10,20s/a/b/'          # lines 10 to 20
sed-rs -e '/^def: /,/^=$/d'      # from one pattern to the next
sed-rs -e '5,/^$/s/x/y/'         # from a line to a pattern
```

**Why:** CHANGES.md lines go under the first header for the day; there
is no way to address only the first match today.

## 3. Literal (fixed-string) patterns: `-F`, or a flag on `s`

```bash
sed-rs -F -e 's/  ." F6 (fn+F6)" cr/  ." Cmd-Enter or F6" cr/'
sed-rs -e 's/a (b) + c/x/L'      # L: the pattern is a literal string
```

Neither the pattern nor the replacement is a regex: `( ) [ ] . * + ? \ |`
and `&` mean themselves.

**Why:** most edits here replace exact code (Forth, Rust, Markdown),
full of these characters. Writing `[(]`, `[+]`, `[.]` is error-prone;
`\(` and `\+` silently became operators through the BRE conversion, and
two of four edits matched nothing.

## 4. Report edits that changed nothing: `--strict`

```bash
sed-rs --strict -i -e 's/old/new/' file   # exit 1, naming the script, if it matched nothing
```

A warning on stderr without `--strict` would also help.

**Why:** an edit that silently matches nothing looks like success; it was
caught only by a `diff` afterwards.


- `\n` in a replacement, to insert a line after a match.
- Several `-e` scripts in one run.
- Rust regex classes and repetition (`[0-9]{4}`, `\s`, `+`).
- The same behaviour on macOS and Linux, which is why the scripts here use

+two of four edits matched nothing.  Later (2026-11-01): `||` in a Rust

+the wrong place; `\{` became an interval (`repetition quantifier expects
+a valid decimal`).  Without `-i`, a failed run under `> file` also leaves
+the file empty, so each of these needed a restore from the `.orig` copy.

| turtle/fractals: classic fractals drawn by recursion with turtle/core
| vim: ft=reva :
|
| Each fractal is a word taking a depth; each `-demo` word clears the
| canvas, places the turtle and sizes the step so the figure fills the
| window.  Depths are capped (see `?depth`) so a typo cannot ask for
| billions of lines; the turtle itself stops drawing at 1,000,000.
|
|   koch-demo  sierpinski-demo  dragon-demo  hilbert-demo  tree-demo
|   plant-demo  fractals ( lists them )
|
| The fractals are written the Logo way, drawing while they recurse.  The
| step length shrinks exactly ( `1 3 scale` ), and `tpush`/`tpop` save
| and restore the whole turtle, step included.

needs turtle/core
push~
~turtle

: ?depth ( n max -- n ) 2dup > if ." (depth capped at " dup . ." ) " then min 0 max ;

| Koch curve: each edge becomes four edges a third as long
: koch ( depth -- )
    dup 0if drop step ;then
    1- dup koch 60 left dup koch 120 right dup koch 60 left koch ;
: snowflake ( depth -- ) 3 0do dup koch 120 right loop drop ;
: koch-demo ( depth -- )
    7 ?depth clear blue color
    penup -270 156 setxy 90 setheading pendown
    540 step! dup 0do 1 3 scale loop snowflake ;

| Sierpinski triangle: three half-size triangles in the corners
: (tri) ( -- ) 3 0do step 120 left loop ;
: sierpinski ( depth -- )
    dup 0if drop (tri) ;then
    1- tpush 1 2 scale
    tpush dup sierpinski tpop
    tpush penup step pendown dup sierpinski tpop
    penup 60 left step 60 right pendown sierpinski
    tpop ;
: sierpinski-demo ( depth -- )
    8 ?depth clear purple color
    penup -350 -300 setxy 90 setheading pendown
    700 step! sierpinski ;

| Dragon curve: fold a strip of paper in half n times, unfold at 90 degrees
: dragon ( depth sign -- )
    over 0if 2drop step ;then
    >r 1- dup 1 dragon r@ 90 * right -1 dragon r> drop ;
: dragon-demo ( depth -- )
    16 ?depth clear orange color
    penup -200 -80 setxy 90 over 45 * - setheading pendown
    480 step! dup 0do 70711 100000 scale loop 1 dragon ;

| Hilbert curve: a path through every cell of a 2^n x 2^n grid
: (h) ( n a -- n a n' a ) 2dup swap 1- swap ;
: hilbert ( depth angle -- )
    over 0if 2drop ;then
    dup right (h) negate hilbert step
    dup left (h) hilbert step
    (h) hilbert dup left step
    (h) negate hilbert right drop ;
: hilbert-demo ( depth -- )
    8 ?depth clear green color
    penup -320 -320 setxy 0 setheading pendown
    640 step! 1 over 1 swap << 1- scale 90 hilbert ;

| Fractal tree: a trunk and two smaller trees, thinner and greener
: tree ( len depth -- )
    dup 0if 2drop ;then
    tpush
    dup 2 > if brown else green then color  dup width
    over forward
    25 left  over 2 3 */ over 1- tree
    50 right over 2 3 */ over 1- tree
    2drop tpop ;
: tree-demo ( depth -- )
    12 ?depth clear
    penup 0 -380 setxy 0 setheading pendown
    170 swap tree 1 width ;

| A small L-system interpreter: a rule per character, expanded by
| recursion (no strings are built).  F and G draw a step, f moves a step,
| + and - turn by `angle`, [ and ] save and restore the turtle.
create rules 128 2* cells allot
variable angle
: rules-clear ( -- ) rules 128 2* cells 0 fill ;
: rule ( c a n -- ) rot 127 and 2* cells rules + tuck ! cell+ ! ;
: rule@ ( c -- a n ) 127 and 2* cells rules + dup cell+ @ swap @ ;
: (draw) ( c -- )
    dup 'F = over 'G = or if drop step ;then
    dup 'f = if drop penup step pendown ;then
    dup '+ = if drop angle @ right ;then
    dup '- = if drop angle @ left ;then
    dup '[ = if drop tpush ;then
    dup '] = if drop tpop ;then
    drop ;
: lsys ( a n depth -- )
    -rot bounds ?do
        i c@ over 0if (draw) else
            dup rule@ nip if over 1- swap rule@ rot lsys else (draw) then
        then
    loop drop ;
: plant-demo ( depth -- )
    6 ?depth clear green color
    rules-clear 25 angle !
    'X " F+[[X]-X]-F[-FX]+X" rule
    'F " FF" rule
    penup -150 -390 setxy 25 setheading pendown
    4 step! 1 over 6 swap - 1 swap << * 1 scale
    " X" rot lsys ;

: fractals ( -- )
    ." Try (depth first):" cr
    ."   5 koch-demo   6 sierpinski-demo   12 dragon-demo" cr
    ."   6 hilbert-demo   10 tree-demo   5 plant-demo" cr
    ." Save the drawing:  \" fractal.svg\" svg-save ." cr ;

pop~

lines: -    ." Save the drawing:  \" fractal.svg\" svg-save ." cr ;
+    ." Save the drawing:  \" fractal.svg\" svg-save ." cr
+    ." (The CLI has no window: it writes each drawing to a new" cr
+    ."  turtle-NNN.svg or .png itself; see reva --help, --draw.)" cr ;

# Reva Forth — portable core

A Rust port of the Reva Forth core that runs on any 64-bit host and in the
browser (WebAssembly), while running Reva's own Forth source — including the
words written as x86 machine code — unchanged.

It does this by executing the small subset of 32-bit x86 that Reva's compiler
and primitives use (a "vx86" VM), with the assembly core's routines
re-implemented in Rust. See [design.md](../docs/design.md) for the rationale.

## Status

- All of `src/reva.f` boots verbatim (assembler, contexts, `needs`, the
  FFI layer, the Linux personality) and restarts as its saved executable
  did: banner, `ok>` prompt, `reva.f`'s error handling. See design.md §3.6.
- `needs` loads libraries from `lib/` (via the virtual prefix `/reva/lib/`;
  set `$REVA_HOME` to use another tree).
- A virtual libc (`getenv`, `putenv`, `localtime`, `opendir`/`readdir`)
  and a portable `syscall` subset; `time&date`, `ms@`, `getenv` work.
- File words (`open/r`, `read`, `seek`, `stat`, `rename`, …) through
  `Host::fs`: real files on the CLI, an in-memory file system in the
  browser (kept in `localStorage`); `lib/` is built in. See design.md §3.7.
- Hosts: `reva` CLI (Linux/macOS/Windows, any CPU) and a WebAssembly module
  with a minimal web console; the VM runs in a Web Worker with time slices
  and a Stop button (design.md §3.8).
- Saved images: `save NAME` from Forth or `reva --save-image`; start one
  with `reva --image` or in the browser (`start(..., { image })`).
  `restart` makes the VM again the same way (design.md §3.9).
- x87 floating point with `f64` registers and 80-bit memory operands;
  `lib/math/floats` passes its own tests (design.md §3.10).
- Not yet: native libraries, native translation. See the roadmap in design.md.

## Layout

One Cargo workspace per component (the rules: [code-metrics.md](../docs/code-metrics.md)),
each `components/<name>/` with its `Cargo.toml`, `Cargo.lock` and
`crates/<crate>/`. All of them build into the repository's `target/`.

```
components/
  macros/   reva-macros  machine_trait!, words!, ext_trait!
  x86-types/  reva-x86-base, -mem, -fpustate, -types   faults, layout, memory, x87 registers, Op/Insn/Cpu
  x86-decode/ reva-x86-cursor, -opcodes, -fpudec, -decode   the decoder (an opcode table)
  x86-alu/    reva-x86-ops, -shift, -float              operands, ALU, shifts, strings, x87 math
  x86-exec/   reva-x86-fpuexec, -exec                   executing instructions
  x86/      reva-x86     facade: the x86 components under their old paths
  host-base/ reva-version, -embedded, -hostcall, -charset   build stamp, reva.f and lib/, host calls, encodings
  vfs/      reva-vfs, reva-memtree, reva-memfs         file-system traits, the in-memory file system
  host/     reva-host-traits, -buffer, reva-host       the Host traits, BufferHost, a facade at the old paths
  core-parts/ reva-gate, reva-heap, reva-translate   gates, the heap allocator, translator hooks
  canvas/   reva-canvas, reva-canvas-out           the turtle's display list; ops for windows, SVG
  ui/       reva-ui-base, -text, -tree, reva-ui   the model of IUP programs' UIs (../docs/ui-model.md)
  ui-layout/ reva-ui-layout   IUP's layout of the model, in character cells
  ui-grid/  reva-ui-mirror, -grid, -paint   the TUI: the model painted into character cells
  ui-web/   reva-ui-web     the TUI in the page (Yew; scripts/build-web.sh)
  iup/      reva-vlib-iup, reva-ui-script, reva-ui-term   the virtual library iup; a
                         scripted headless UI host; the TUI in the terminal (crossterm)
  core/     reva-core, -ffi, -inspect              the Machine and its helpers; (call) args; dictionary, state
  core-run/ reva-core-run, reva-core-boot          the run loop; new machines and images
  vlib/     reva-vlib-turtle, -highlight, -iconv, reva-vlib   virtual libraries (reva-vlib: the old paths)
  words-base/   reva-words-code, -text, -calls, -scan   the words' helpers
  words-interp/ reva-words-classes, -interp, -eval      classes, interpreter, eval, catch, defining
  words-dict/   reva-words-compile, -memory, -system    compiling, numbers, memory, bye/version
  words-os/     reva-words-sys, -files, -libc, -ffi     system calls, file words, libc, (call)
  words/    reva-words   the dispatch table: every gate to its handler
  vm/       reva-vm      the facade the front ends use (re-exports, Machine with
                         dispatch installed; ../docs/design.md 3.12)
  sqlite/   reva-sqlite, reva-vlib-sqlite   SQLite (rusqlite, safe API); the virtual library
  cli-edit/ reva-keys, -history, -lineedit, -rawterm   the terminal line editor
  cli-host/ reva-hostpath, -stdfs, -term, -stdhost     the command-line host
  cli/      reva-cli     the `reva` command: options, run, session
  web/      reva-web-state, -run, -io, reva-web   wasm32 module + www/ (reva.js,
                         index.html) + test/*.mjs
  serve/    reva-serve-http, reva-serve   one-binary local web app: embeds a site,
                         serves 127.0.0.1 (std only; ../docs/serve.md)
  desktop/  reva-desktop-pkg, -state, reva-desktop   the Tauri app, with build.sh,
                         smoke.sh, host.js
scripts/      build-web.sh, regress.sh, add-regress.sh, check.sh, bench-guard.sh,
              doc-check.sh (run docs/ samples), parity-examples.sh, ...
tests/forth/  Forth scripts used by the regression suite
work/reg-rs/  reg-rs regression tests (.rgt specs + golden .out/.err)
```

## Build and run

From the repository root:

```bash
just cli                                  # or: cargo build --release --manifest-path components/cli/Cargo.toml
target/release/reva                       # REPL (ok> prompt)
target/release/reva file.f -e '...'       # include files, evaluate text
echo ': sq dup * ; 7 sq .' | target/release/reva
target/release/reva --help
```

WebAssembly:

```bash
scripts/build-web.sh                      # → components/web/crates/reva-web/www/reva.wasm
python3 -m http.server -d components/web/crates/reva-web/www    # open http://localhost:8000
node components/web/crates/reva-web/test/smoke.mjs              # headless check
scripts/make-web-zip.sh                   # → target/web/reva-web-VERSION.zip (../docs/web.md)
scripts/build-serve.sh                    # → target/serve/reva-serve-VERSION-TARGET (../docs/serve.md)
```

## Tests

The gate before every commit, from the repository root:

```bash
just check            # fmt, clippy, tests, wasm + node tests, desktop, goldens, licenses, sw-checklist
just check --fast     # the same without the desktop component
```

`scripts/check.sh` lists the goldens known to fail on each OS (the list
may only shrink) and requires sw-checklist to report no FAILs.

Refactors of hot code (gate dispatch, decode, exec) also run the timing
guard before and after:

```bash
just bench-guard            # boot, fib, a loop, dragons: medians vs this host's baseline
just bench-guard --record   # (re)record this host's baseline in work/bench-guard.txt
```

It fails when a median is more than 15% (`TOLERANCE`) slower than the
host's recorded baseline; timings only compare on the same machine, so
each host has its own lines. It is not part of `just check` (it takes
about 17 s and timing is noisy on a busy machine). The pieces of the
gate:

```bash
just test                                 # unit + API tests, every component
scripts/regress.sh                        # reg-rs golden-output suite
scripts/regress.sh -vv -p core-catch      # one test, full diff on failure
REVA=target/release/reva scripts/regress.sh
```

The regression suite uses [reg-rs](https://github.com/sw-cli-tools/reg-rs)
(`reg-rs` on PATH, or `REG_RS=/path/to/reg-rs`). Add a test with

```bash
scripts/add-regress.sh NAME '${REVA:-target/debug/reva} < tests/forth/NAME.f' 'what it covers'
```

and review the captured `work/reg-rs/NAME.out` before committing: a baseline
asserts the output is *correct*. Accept an intended change with
`REG_RS_DATA_DIR=work/reg-rs reg-rs rebase -p NAME`.

Source as color-highlighted HTML or PNG, for slides, docs and blog figures
(Python 3 standard library; `--png` uses headless Chrome or Chromium):

```bash

```

# Reva Forth — portable core

A Rust port of the Reva Forth core that runs on any 64-bit host and in the
browser (WebAssembly), while running Reva's own Forth source — including the
words written as x86 machine code — unchanged.

It does this by executing the small subset of 32-bit x86 that Reva's compiler
and primitives use (a "vx86" VM), with the assembly core's routines
re-implemented in Rust. See [design.md](../docs/design.md) for the rationale.

## Status

- All of `src/reva.f` boots verbatim (assembler, contexts, `needs`, the
  FFI layer, the Linux personality) and restarts as its saved executable
  did: banner, `ok>` prompt, `reva.f`'s error handling. See design.md §3.6.
- `needs` loads libraries from `lib/` (via the virtual prefix `/reva/lib/`;
  set `$REVA_HOME` to use another tree).
- A virtual libc (`getenv`, `putenv`, `localtime`, `opendir`/`readdir`)
  and a portable `syscall` subset; `time&date`, `ms@`, `getenv` work.
- File words (`open/r`, `read`, `seek`, `stat`, `rename`, …) through
  `Host::fs`: real files on the CLI, an in-memory file system in the
  browser (kept in `localStorage`); `lib/` is built in. See design.md §3.7.
- Hosts: `reva` CLI (Linux/macOS/Windows, any CPU) and a WebAssembly module
  with a minimal web console; the VM runs in a Web Worker with time slices
  and a Stop button (design.md §3.8).
- Saved images: `save NAME` from Forth or `reva --save-image`; start one
  with `reva --image` or in the browser (`start(..., { image })`).
  `restart` makes the VM again the same way (design.md §3.9).
- x87 floating point with `f64` registers and 80-bit memory operands;
  `lib/math/floats` passes its own tests (design.md §3.10).
- Not yet: native libraries, native translation. See the roadmap in design.md.

## Layout

One Cargo workspace per component (the rules: [code-metrics.md](../docs/code-metrics.md)),
each `components/<name>/` with its `Cargo.toml`, `Cargo.lock` and
`crates/<crate>/`. All of them build into the repository's `target/`.

```
  x86-decode/ reva-x86-cursor, -opcodes, -fpudec, -decode   the decoder (an opcode table)
  x86-alu/    reva-x86-ops, -shift, -float              operands, ALU, shifts, strings, x87 math
  x86-exec/   reva-x86-fpuexec, -exec                   executing instructions
  x86/      reva-x86     facade: the x86 components under their old paths
  host-base/ reva-version, -embedded, -hostcall, -charset   build stamp, reva.f and lib/, host calls, encodings
  vfs/      reva-vfs, reva-memtree, reva-memfs         file-system traits, the in-memory file system
  host/     reva-host-traits, -buffer, reva-host       the Host traits, BufferHost, a facade at the old paths
  core-parts/ reva-gate, reva-heap, reva-translate   gates, the heap allocator, translator hooks
  canvas/   reva-canvas, -out, -png                the turtle's display list; ops for windows, SVG, PNG
  ui/       reva-ui-base, -text, -tree, reva-ui   the model of IUP programs' UIs (../docs/ui-model.md)
  ui-layout/ reva-ui-layout   IUP's layout of the model, in character cells

  core-run/ reva-core-run, reva-core-boot          the run loop; new machines and images
  vlib/     reva-vlib-turtle, -highlight, -iconv, reva-vlib   virtual libraries (reva-vlib: the old paths)
  words-base/   reva-words-code, -text, -calls, -scan   the words' helpers

                         index.html) + test/*.mjs

              doc-check.sh (run docs/ samples), parity-examples.sh, ...

```

## Build and run

From the repository root:

```bash
just cli                                  # or: cargo build --release --manifest-path components/cli/Cargo.toml
target/release/reva                       # REPL (ok> prompt)
target/release/reva file.f -e '...'       # include files, evaluate text
echo ': sq dup * ; 7 sq .' | target/release/reva
target/release/reva --help
```

WebAssembly:

```bash
scripts/build-web.sh                      # → components/web/crates/reva-web/www/reva.wasm
python3 -m http.server -d components/web/crates/reva-web/www    # open http://localhost:8000
node components/web/crates/reva-web/test/smoke.mjs              # headless check
scripts/make-web-zip.sh                   # → target/web/reva-web-VERSION.zip (../docs/web.md)
scripts/build-serve.sh                    # → target/serve/reva-serve-VERSION-TARGET (../docs/serve.md)
```

## Tests

The gate before every commit, from the repository root:

```bash
just check            # fmt, clippy, tests, wasm + node tests, desktop, goldens, licenses, sw-checklist
just check --fast     # the same without the desktop component
```

`scripts/check.sh` lists the goldens known to fail on each OS (the list
may only shrink) and requires sw-checklist to report no FAILs.

Refactors of hot code (gate dispatch, decode, exec) also run the timing
guard before and after:

```bash
just bench-guard            # boot, fib, a loop, dragons: medians vs this host's baseline
just bench-guard --record   # (re)record this host's baseline in work/bench-guard.txt
```

It fails when a median is more than 15% (`TOLERANCE`) slower than the
host's recorded baseline; timings only compare on the same machine, so
each host has its own lines. It is not part of `just check` (it takes
about 17 s and timing is noisy on a busy machine). The pieces of the
gate:

```bash
just test                                 # unit + API tests, every component
scripts/regress.sh                        # reg-rs golden-output suite
scripts/regress.sh -vv -p core-catch      # one test, full diff on failure

```

The regression suite uses [reg-rs](https://github.com/sw-cli-tools/reg-rs)
(`reg-rs` on PATH, or `REG_RS=/path/to/reg-rs`). Add a test with

```bash
scripts/add-regress.sh NAME '${REVA:-target/debug/reva} < tests/forth/NAME.f' 'what it covers'
```

and review the captured `work/reg-rs/NAME.out` before committing: a baseline
asserts the output is *correct*. Accept an intended change with
`REG_RS_DATA_DIR=work/reg-rs reg-rs rebase -p NAME`.

Source as color-highlighted HTML or PNG, for slides, docs and blog figures
(Python 3 standard library; `--png` uses headless Chrome or Chromium):


< # Portable Reva core — design
< 
< This document explains *why* the port looks the way it does. For *how to
< use it*, see [README.md](README.md).
< 
< ## 1. Problem
< 
< Reva is a 32-bit x86 Forth:
< 
< - the core (`src/newcore.asm`, ~2,000 lines, plus one ~550-line OS layer
<   per platform) is NASM assembly;
< - the compiler emits x86 machine code directly (`compile` writes
<   `call rel32`, `literal` writes a 10-byte push sequence, `if` writes
<   `test eax,eax; lodsd; jz rel32`, `;` turns a trailing call into a jump);
< - about 60 words in `src/reva.f` and about 100 in the libraries are
<   *written* as instruction bytes (`: + inline{ 01 06 } drop ;inline`).
< 
< 32-bit x86 is going away (macOS dropped it in 10.15; 64-bit Linux needs
< multilib), and none of it can run in a browser.
< 
< ## 2. Options considered
< 
< | Option | Reuse of existing Forth | Native speed | Browser | Cost |
< |---|---|---|---|---|
< | Token-threaded Rust VM | low: every machine-code word, every control structure and the compiler must be rewritten | interpreter, 2–5× slower | yes | high |
< | Hand-written x86-64 / ARM64 assembly cores | low (same rewrite, twice) | yes | no | very high |
< | **vx86: run Reva's IA-32 subset in a Rust VM** (chosen) | **high: `reva.f` runs byte-for-byte** | interpreter now; native via translation (§6) | yes | medium |
< 
< The deciding observation: Reva's world is already a *flat 32-bit address
< space with fixed register roles* — exactly what `wasm32` linear memory is,
< and what a 64-bit host can model with one base register. Reva's compiled
< code uses only a small, regular slice of IA-32. Executing that slice is
< far less work than rewriting everything that produces it.
< 
< ## 3. Architecture
< 
< ```
<             ┌──────────── hosts ────────────┐
<             │  reva-cli (terminal, StdFs)    │   push input, pull output,
<             │  reva-web (wasm32, MemFs, JS)  │   run in budgeted slices
<             └───────────────┬────────────────┘
<                             │ Host trait, Status
< ┌───────────────────────────▼──────────────────────────────┐
< │ reva-vm                                                    │
< │  machine   dispatcher: step = one instruction or gateway   │
< │  x86       decode (bytes → Insn, cached) + exec (Cpu)      │
< │  gates     newcore.asm routines in Rust, at fixed addrs    │
< │  mem       flat u32-addressed memory, code-page tracking   │
< │  heap      allocate/free/resize                            │
< │  ffi       virtual libc, Linux syscall subset              │
< │  fileio    file words + file syscalls over Host::fs        │
< │  vfs       FileSystem trait, MemFs, embedded lib/          │
< │  image     save/load (vx86 bytes only)                     │
< │  translate hooks for native/wasm translators               │
< └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
< ```
< 
< ### 3.1 Memory and registers
< 
< One `Vec<u8>`; every address Forth sees is an offset into it
< (`layout.rs` has the map, mirroring newcore's data section). Registers keep
< Reva's roles: **EAX = top of stack, ESI = data-stack pointer, ESP = return
< stack** (in VM memory, so `r>` on a return address works as it always did).
< Addresses below 0x1000 fault, so `0 @` is reported, not silently read.
< 
< ### 3.2 The instruction subset
< 
< The decoder (components/x86-decode) covers the one-byte and `0F` opcodes that occur in Reva's
< output and sources, plus their regular neighbours: all ALU ops in all
< forms, shifts/rotates, `mul/imul/div/idiv`, `lods/stos/movs/scas/cmps` with
< `rep`, near `jmp/call/ret/jcc/loop`, `setcc/cmovcc`, `movzx/movsx`, `66`
< prefix, and the x87 floating-point unit (§3.10). Flags are exact except AF.
< Anything else faults with the bytes and the Forth word containing them. Not
< modelled, deliberately: segments, privileged/system instructions, MMX/SSE.
< 
< ### 3.3 Gateways: the core in Rust
< 
< Each newcore routine is a `Gate` at `0x1000 + 4n`. Compiled code reaches
< it by `call`/`jmp`/`call [vector]` exactly as before; the dispatcher runs
< Rust instead of decoding bytes. Dictionary entries keep newcore's layout
< `[class][link][xt][count][name]`, class handlers are gateways, DEFER
< vectors are cells holding addresses — so `reva.f` code that manipulates
< any of these keeps working.
< 
< Where an assembly routine fell through into the next (`cclass` into
< `vclass`, `cold` into `bye`, `literal` into `comma`), the Rust keeps the
< combined behaviour; comments in the word families (components/words-*) name each case.
< 
< ### 3.4 Never blocking: continuation gateways
< 
< A browser cannot block in `key`. So any routine that calls back into Forth
< (interpret, query, eval, include, catch, `:` via the `(header)` vector) is
< split at each call: the call becomes "push continuation gateway *k*, jump
< to target", and the rest of the routine is *k*. No Forth state lives on the
< Rust stack, so `run()` can return `NeedInput` (or `Yielded` when its budget
< is spent) after any step and resume later. The CLI and the browser use the
< same core.
< 
< Rarely-hooked callbacks (`do_cr`, `prompt`, `iterate`, user `emit`/`type`)
< run as *nested calls* on the Rust stack; if one asks for input that is not
< queued, a blocking host may supply it, otherwise it faults clearly.
< 
< ### 3.5 Self-modifying code
< 
< Reva patches code (`then`, tail calls, `does>`). Decoded instructions are
< cached per address; memory marks 256-byte pages that hold decoded code, and
< a write into such a page queues it for invalidation (decode cache and any
< translator). Writes to data pages cost one bit test.
< 
< ### 3.6 Booting all of `reva.f`, and what stands in for its last step
< 
< `reva.f` is a build script: it compiles the whole system, then saves a new
< native executable with `(save)` and exits. The saved executable, when run,
< starts with fresh stacks, runs the `onstartup` list (which allocates
< `scratch`, `pad` and the compiled-string area) and calls `appstart` (banner,
< command line, then the `catch`-protected interpreter loop).
< 
< The port boots `reva.f` verbatim up to that last step, then does in place
< what "save and run the executable" did (`embedded::boot_source`):
< 
< 1. Before `reva.f` hides `(compstr)`, one inserted line hands the string area
<    to `setextra`, exactly as `save` does, so the startup code finds the
<    strings compiled during the boot.
< 2. Instead of `(save) bye`, the tail runs `(boot-restart)`: drop the boot
<    file from `argv`, abandon the include frames, and jump to `cold`. It is
<    also given `reva.f`'s interpreter loop (`exception-reset`), so fault
<    recovery returns to the same loop rather than the core's bare REPL.
< 
< Why not implement `(save)` and run the result? A browser cannot exec a file,
< and the image would be identical to the memory we already have. A saved
< image is the portable form of that executable: it starts the same way, and
< `(save)` writes one (§3.9).
< 
< **Virtual install prefix.** The core reports its program path as
< `/reva/bin/lin/reva`, the original layout, so `reva.f`'s `libdir` gives
< `/reva/lib/` without changing a line. Hosts map `/reva/` to real files: the
< CLI to `$REVA_HOME` or the checkout it was built from; every host also sees
< the copy of `lib/` compiled into the core (§3.7).
< 
< **The OS layer (`ffi.rs`).** `reva.f` selects its Linux personality
< (`os` = 1) and reaches the OS through `lib`/`func:` and `syscall`. The port
< serves one virtual library, libc, whose functions (`getenv`, `putenv`,
< `localtime`, `errno`) are gateways over `Host`; any other library or
< function resolves to 0, as a failed `dlopen`/`dlsym` did, so `reva.f` names
< what is missing, and the VM adds a one-line note naming the library
< (`Host::diag`; stderr on the CLI). `system` is served but runs only where
< the host allows it (`Host::system`: the CLI with `--allow-shell`, never the
< browser); otherwise it faults with how to allow it. Linux i386 `syscall` numbers used outside file I/O (time,
< `gettimeofday`, `nanosleep`, `getpid`, terminal `ioctl`) map to `Host`; the
< rest return `-ENOSYS`. The VM itself never reads a clock or the environment,
< so it stays deterministic and the browser host needs nothing.
< 
< ### 3.7 Files
< 
< `reva.f`'s file words bottom out in newcore's `open/r`, `open/rw`, `creat`,
< `close`, `read`, `write`, `fsize`, and in Linux system calls (`lseek`,
< `rename`, `unlink`, `stat`, `chdir`, `getcwd`; `mkdir`/`rmdir` and
< `opendir`/`readdir` in `lib/os/dir`). The port keeps both layers as they
< are and implements the bottom one (`fileio.rs`) over a small trait,
< `vfs::FileSystem` (open/close/read/write/seek/stat/remove/rename/mkdir/
< rmdir/list/chdir/cwd), that a host lends through `Host::fs`:
< 
< - **CLI:** `StdFs`, the real file system; `/reva/` maps to the install
<   root. Descriptors are the host's own numbers (from 3), not OS fds.
<   VM paths are always `/`-rooted and `/`-separated; on Windows the host
<   path `C:\dir` is the VM path `/C:/dir` and back (`vm_path`/`host_path`
<   in reva-hostpath's `paths.rs`), so one `vfs::normalize` serves every host.
< - **Browser and tests:** `MemFs`, an in-memory tree. It records which
<   paths changed, and `reva-web` exports them so `reva.js` can keep them in
<   `localStorage` and put them back before the next boot. A page bundles
<   its own files the same way (`Reva.load(url, { files, storage })`).
< 
< Results follow the kernel: a value or `-errno`, and `ioerr` is 0 or the
< negative result, exactly as newcore's `call_linux_return` left it, so
< library code that tests `ioerr` behaves as before. Descriptors 0–2 stay
< the console (writing to 1 or 2 is output).
< 
< **`lib/` is embedded** (`build.rs`, feature `embed-lib`, on by default) and
< appears read-only at `/reva/lib/` under both file systems: `needs` works in
< the browser with no fetches, and an installed CLI binary needs no
< checkout. On the CLI a file on disk wins over the embedded copy; in
< `MemFs` the first write copies an embedded file. Cost: about 0.7 MB in the
< binary and the `.wasm` (text, so it compresses well when served gzipped);
< a host that does not want it builds without the feature.
< 
< Why a trait rather than more `Host` methods? The operations come as a set
< with shared state (open descriptors, working directory), and the same
< `MemFs` serves the browser and every test; the trait keeps that state out
< of the VM, which stays deterministic and image-safe (open files and
< directory streams are host state, not part of an image).
< 
< ### 3.8 The browser: a worker, time slices, interrupt
< 
< The page must never wait for the VM. Booting `reva.f` is one call of
< 140 to 300 ms that cannot be sliced, and a step budget is not a time
< budget (200k steps is 8 ms on a desktop, several times that on a phone).
< So the browser host runs the VM in a **Web Worker** (`www/reva-worker.js`)
< and the page only draws and stores (`www/reva.js` `start()`):
< 
< - **Time slices.** `Reva.run` runs 50k-step chunks until about 8 ms have
<   passed, posts the output, and yields. Yields use a `MessageChannel`
<   message (no 4 ms timer clamp), but at least every 25 ms a `setTimeout`,
<   because a port's messages can starve other tasks (Node does this, and
<   `scheduler.yield()` does it by design). That fair turn is what lets
<   `input` and `stop` messages in while the VM computes. Measured: about 90%
<   of the unsliced speed.
< - **Messages:** `init`, `input`, `close`, `stop` to the worker; `output`,
<   `status`, `files`, `error` back (table in `reva-worker.js`). Workers
<   cannot see `localStorage`, so changed files travel to the page, which
<   saves them whenever the VM waits for input or halts.
< - **Drawing:** the page appends output at most once per animation frame and
<   caps the console's length.
< - **Input** never blocks a thread: `key` returns `NEED_INPUT` and the
<   worker is idle until the next `input` message.
< - **Interrupt:** `Machine::interrupt` (`reva_interrupt`) is taken at the
<   next step of `run`: queued input is dropped and the VM recovers as from a
<   fault (`*** interrupted (in WORD)`), keeping the dictionary. Code inside
<   a nested call runs to completion within one step, so if the worker does
<   not answer in 2 s the page terminates it and starts a fresh one.
< - **Clock:** the module has no imports, so the page passes `Date.now()` in
<   (`reva_set_time`) before each slice; tests keep the fixed clock, and the
<   smoke test checks that 1k- and 1M-step slices print the same transcript.
< - **Fallback:** where a worker cannot start, the same loop runs on the
<   page's thread, using `scheduler.yield()` to let the page draw.
< 
< No `SharedArrayBuffer` or `Atomics.wait` (they need COOP/COEP headers that
< a plain static server does not send), so any static directory serves it.
< 
< ### 3.9 Saved images and `restart`
< 
< Reva turned a program into an executable with `save NAME` (`(save)` under
< it) and relaunched itself with `restart`. Both are host matters here.
< 
< - **Images.** `(save)` ( a n -- ) writes the machine's state as an image
<   (`image.rs`: statics, dictionary, code, heap; vx86 bytes only) to the
<   named file through `Host::fs`, with `ioerr` as for the file words.
<   `reva.f`'s `save` wrapper runs unchanged around it (it hands over the
<   compiled-string area and prints the sizes). `save` may run from a file
<   being included or inside a word; loading an image therefore resets the
<   interpreter's source, `>in`, compile state and catch frame, as a freshly
<   started executable had them, and starts at `cold`. `reva --save-image`
<   writes the same format from outside.
< - **Starting from one.** `reva --image FILE`; in the browser
<   `start(wasm, { image })` (a URL or bytes; the worker fetches it), or
<   `reva_boot_image` in the module's C ABI. An image skips compiling
<   `reva.f` and whatever was loaded before saving, which is what a
<   page needs to start a large program at once.
< - **`restart`** is a core word (gate appended after the libc gates, so
<   image addresses stay stable). It runs the `onexit` list as `bye` does,
<   then the machine stops with `Status::Restart`. The host keeps a
<   `reva_vm::Start`, the way it made the machine (boot with `argv`, or
<   image bytes), makes a new machine from it, and hands over the input not
<   yet read (`Machine::take_input`; the rest of the current line is gone,
<   as it was in the old process). What the host owns survives: files, and
<   the console. The CLI then includes its files and evaluates its `-e`
<   texts again; the browser module does all of this inside `reva_run`, so
<   JavaScript sees only output (a new banner). This replaces wrapper loops
<   that relaunch on a special exit status.
< - **Why the host and not the VM.** A restart is "run the program again"; a
<   VM that reset itself would have to know how it was made (boot file,
<   image, arguments) and would mix host policy into the core. One `Start`
<   type keeps it identical on every host.
< 
< A script that calls `restart` unconditionally restarts for ever, as it did
< on the original (and as a launcher loop would); stop it with Ctrl-C.
< 
< ### 3.10 Floating point: the x87
< 
< `lib/math/floats` is x87 code written as bytes (`f+` is `inline{ de c1 }`,
< `f@` is `fld tbyte [eax]`), and CoSy stores its floats in the x87's 80-bit
< format. So the VM decodes the x87 (`D8`–`DF`, `fwait` as a no-op;
< components/x86-exec's reva-x86-fpuexec) and keeps its state in the CPU: eight registers as a stack
< with `TOP` and tags, the control word and the status word.
< 
< - **What is there:** loads and stores of every memory format (32/64/80-bit
<   floats, 16/32/64-bit integers, `fisttp`), constants, the four
<   operations in all their forms, compares (`fcom`, `fucom`, `fcomi`,
<   `ftst`, `fxam`, condition codes `C0`–`C3`), `fxch`, `ffree`, `fcmov`,
<   `fldcw`/`fstcw`/`fstsw`, `finit`/`fclex`, and the transcendentals
<   (`fsin`, `fcos`, `fsincos`, `fptan`, `fpatan`, `f2xm1`, `fyl2x`,
<   `fyl2xp1`, `fscale`, `fxtract`, `fprem`, `fprem1`, `frndint`, `fsqrt`).
<   Not there: `fldenv`/`fstenv`/`fsave`/`frstor` and the BCD forms.
< - **Registers are `f64`.** A software 80-bit float would be exact but slow
<   and large, and every host has a fast IEEE double. 80-bit memory values
<   convert exactly to the 80-bit format and round to nearest-even on the
<   way in; 64-bit integers round like doubles. Arithmetic rounds to double
<   whatever the precision field says, and the rounding field applies to
<   `fist`/`frndint` only. Results can differ from a real x87 in the last
<   bits of the extended format, which shows when a program prints more
<   digits than a double holds, or truncates (`f.` prints `0.49999` for
<   `sin 30°`).
< - **Exceptions are masked**, as Reva left them: an invalid operation gives
<   the indefinite NaN and sets `IE`, an empty register reads as a stack
<   fault, a push onto a full stack overflows to NaN, and `fwait` never
<   traps. The sticky flags are visible through `fstsw`.
< - **No new imports:** the WebAssembly module still imports nothing; the
<   `f64` functions come from Rust's standard library.
< - The FPU state is part of the CPU, not of an image: a saved program starts
<   with a fresh unit, as a new process did (`finit` state).
< 
< ### 3.11 Host calls and SQLite
< 
< Decided with the user on 2026-10-26 (saga steps `local-sqlite-design`,
< `local-sqlite`):
< 
< - **SQLite on every host.** The CLI and the desktop app use SQLite
<   compiled into the native binary; the browser uses SQLite's official
<   WebAssembly build ([sqlite.org/wasm](https://sqlite.org/wasm)) loaded by
<   the page, with databases kept in the browser's private file system
<   (OPFS). `lib/db/sqlite` programs run unchanged on all three.
< - **No C calls in our code.** Native hosts use the `reva-sqlite` crate
<   (components/sqlite), which drives SQLite through **rusqlite's safe API**;
<   `libsqlite3-sys` (rusqlite's own dependency) compiles SQLite itself. No
<   `unsafe`, no FFI of ours. `reva-vm` and `reva-web` gain no dependency.
<   The workspace's rust-version is 1.89 (rusqlite 0.41).
< - **No pointers in the Forth binding.** The old `lib/db/sqlite` called
<   SQLite's C API directly: out-parameters (`sqlite3_open` writing the
<   handle through a pointer), returned `char*`, and an x86 `callback:`
<   thunk for `sqlite3_exec`. Nothing else used that layer: programs and
<   libraries use the `~db` words (`sql_open`, `sql_exec`, `sql_prepare`,
<   `sql_pexec`, `sql_pcol_text`, `sql_fetch` ...). So the library now sits
<   on the virtual library `reva-sqlite`, whose functions (`rsql_open`,
<   `rsql_step`, ...) take handles as small integers and strings as
<   `( a n )`; a text answer comes back as its length, with the bytes in a
<   VM buffer (`rsql_ptr`; one per statement and column, so a row's columns
<   stay valid together). `sql_fetch` walks rows with `rsql_next` instead
<   of a C callback, calling the Forth word with a stack of its own as the
<   C callback did. Every public word keeps its stack effect.
< - **Statements without lifetimes.** rusqlite's `Statement` borrows its
<   connection, which does not fit handles kept between Forth calls. A
<   `reva-sqlite` statement keeps its SQL and bindings; its first `step`
<   runs it (rusqlite, safe API) and buffers the rows, later steps hand
<   them out. A SELECT's result is held in memory until reset or finalize,
<   which suits REPL-sized data.
< - **One mechanism, the host call** (`reva_vm::hostcall`). A
<   virtual-library function the VM cannot serve becomes a `HostCall`
<   (service, operation, integers, byte strings: never VM addresses) for
<   `Host::host_call`. The host answers at once (the CLI), later (the
<   desktop's and the browser's worker, which must ask the page), or not at
<   all (a clear stop, as for a native library the core does not serve).
<   "Later" stops the VM with `Status::HostCall`; the host reads
<   `Machine::pending_host_call`, answers with `Machine::resume`, and runs
<   again. Nothing is popped from the data stack until the answer is in,
<   so the call simply retries, as a gateway waiting for input does.
<   - CLI: `reva-sqlite` at once; database names map to host paths as the
<     file words map them.
<   - Desktop: the worker posts the request to the page, the page calls a
<     Tauri command, the native side answers from `reva-sqlite` (paths
<     under the app's folder only), the worker resumes the VM.
<   - Browser: the VM's worker answers itself (`sqlite.js`) with SQLite's
<     official wasm build, loaded from jsDelivr at run time (pinned, not
<     redistributed). Each database runs in memory; opening loads its OPFS
<     file (`sqlite3_deserialize`) and every committed change writes it back
<     (`sqlite3_js_db_export`, a writable stream). SQLite's own OPFS VFSes
<     were tried and rejected: `opfs` needs cross-origin-isolation headers
<     GitHub Pages cannot send, and `opfs-sahpool` holds its files
<     exclusively, so a page kept in the back/forward cache, or a second tab,
<     blocks the next one (seen in Chrome: the reloaded page silently fell
<     back to memory).
< 
<   The same path serves later native services. Gates for the new
<   functions are appended (3.9: images keep gate addresses).
< 
< ### 3.12 Crates
< 
< Decided with the user on 2026-10-27 (saga step `local-crate-layout`): the
< core meets sw-checklist's structure limits in full (at most 7 modules per
< crate, 7 functions per module, 50 lines per function, 500 per file), with
< the bench guard (`just bench-guard`) and every golden unchanged at each
< move.
< 
< Rust allows `impl Machine` only in the crate that defines `Machine`, and
< today eight modules add methods to it. So the split puts `Machine` low and
< lets higher crates extend it:
< 
< | Crate | Holds | State |
< |---|---|---|
< | `reva-x86` | the CPU types, decoder, executor, x87, memory, faults, the memory layout | done (pure moves) |
< | `reva-host` | the `Host` trait and `BufferHost`, host calls, the virtual file system, embedded sources (`reva.f`, `lib/`), version, encodings; owns the build script | done (pure moves) |
< | `reva-core` | `Machine` (state, statics, stacks, heap, images) and the run loop, which dispatches each gate through a table of handler functions instead of one large `match` | next |
< | `reva-words` | the gate handlers by family (interpreter, compiler and dictionary, memory and strings, numbers, files, OS, images, version), as functions over `&mut Machine` | done: the word components (3.13) |
< | `reva-vlib` | the virtual libraries (libc, iconv, SQLite, turtle and canvas, highlight), the same way | later |
< | `reva-vm` | builds the handler table, `Start`, translation hooks, and the public API: every old path is re-exported, so hosts do not change | throughout |
< 
< Dispatch through a table of function pointers replaces the `match` on
< the hot path; the bench guard decides whether that stays.
< 
< ### 3.13 Components
< 
< Decided with the user on 2026-10-28 (saga step `local-components`), after
< sw-mlpl's layout: each part of the core is a *component*, its own Cargo
< workspace under `components/<name>/` with its crates in `crates/`, and
< the structure rules of [code-metrics.md](code-metrics.md) apply (at most
< 4 modules per crate and 4 crates per component; when a part is full, a

# What reva-fork needs from sed-rs

Requests from using [sed-rs](https://github.com/sw-cli-tools/sed-rs) to
edit this repository's files (2026-11-01), most valuable first. Each has
the case that hit it and what would have fixed it.

Today an in-place edit is written as the user's undoable pattern:

```bash
mv file file.orig && sed-rs -e 's/old/new/' < file.orig > file
# wrong? mv file.orig file      right? rm file.orig
```

## 1. In-place editing with a backup: `-i[SUFFIX]`

```bash
sed-rs -i.orig -e 's/old/new/' file      # file.orig keeps the original
sed-rs -i -e 's/old/new/' a.rs b.rs      # several files, no backup
```

- Write the result to a temporary file in the same directory, then rename
  it over the original, so a reader never sees a half-written file.
- If the script does not parse, or any error occurs, leave every file
  untouched and exit non-zero before writing anything.
- Keep the file's permissions.

**Why:** a script that sed-rs rejected ("address ranges are not
supported") still left `> CHANGES.md` truncating the file, and the
command went on to commit an empty CHANGES.md. With `-i`, a failed
script changes nothing.

## 2. Address ranges, and "first match only"

```bash
sed-rs -e '0,/^## 2026-11-01$/s//## 2026-11-01\n\n- new line/'   # first match only
sed-rs -e '10,20s/a/b/'          # lines 10 to 20
sed-rs -e '/^def: /,/^=$/d'      # from one pattern to the next
sed-rs -e '5,/^$/s/x/y/'         # from a line to a pattern
```

**Why:** CHANGES.md lines go under the first header for the day; there
is no way to address only the first match today.

## 3. Literal (fixed-string) patterns: `-F`, or a flag on `s`

```bash
sed-rs -F -e 's/  ." F6 (fn+F6)" cr/  ." Cmd-Enter or F6" cr/'
sed-rs -e 's/a (b) + c/x/L'      # L: the pattern is a literal string
```

Neither the pattern nor the replacement is a regex: `( ) [ ] . * + ? \ |`
and `&` mean themselves.

**Why:** most edits here replace exact code (Forth, Rust, Markdown),
full of these characters. Writing `[(]`, `[+]`, `[.]` is error-prone;
`\(` and `\+` silently became operators through the BRE conversion, and
two of four edits matched nothing.  Later (2026-11-01): `||` in a Rust
pattern matched as an empty alternation and spliced the replacement into
the wrong place; `\{` became an interval (`repetition quantifier expects
a valid decimal`).  Without `-i`, a failed run under `> file` also leaves
the file empty, so each of these needed a restore from the `.orig` copy.

## 4. Report edits that changed nothing: `--strict`

```bash
sed-rs --strict -i -e 's/old/new/' file   # exit 1, naming the script, if it matched nothing
```

A warning on stderr without `--strict` would also help.

**Why:** an edit that silently matches nothing looks like success; it was
caught only by a `diff` afterwards.

## 5. Show the change: `--diff`

```bash
sed-rs -i --diff -e 's/old/new/' file     # edit, and print a unified diff
sed-rs --diff -e 's/old/new/' < file      # dry run: only the diff
```

**Why:** every edit was followed by a separate `diff` to confirm it.

## What already works well

- `\n` in a replacement, to insert a line after a match.
- Several `-e` scripts in one run.
- Rust regex classes and repetition (`[0-9]{4}`, `\s`, `+`).
- The same behaviour on macOS and Linux, which is why the scripts here use
  sed-rs and never the system `sed`.

Step 33 is complete and merged into PR #68 (https://github.com/softwarewrighter/reva-fork/pull/68). Step 34 (`local-cli-drawings`) is built and its full gate, desktop included, is running. When it passes I'll commit, complete step 34 and open its PR on top of #68.

How step 34 works: after each line you type (and after `-e`, files or piped input), a drawing that changed is written to the next free `turtle-001.svg`, `turtle-002.svg`, … in the current folder. An existing file is never overwritten, and an unchanged drawing isn't written again. The file name prints above the prompt (`drawing: turtle-001.svg`).

`--draw` picks the behaviour:

| `--draw` | What happens |
|---|---|
| `auto` (default) | At a terminal: SVG; in iTerm2 or WezTerm a PNG that should also appear inline in the terminal. When output is redirected: nothing, so scripts and goldens are unaffected. |
| `svg` | SVG files, also when output is redirected |
| `png` | 800×800 PNG files |
| `off` | no files; `svg-save` still writes one by name |

**Checked so far:**
- `10 tree-demo` and `6 hilbert-demo` render correctly as PNG; I looked at both images.
